summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the amount lent investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and accordingly by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972 it dismissed the appeals. In doing so the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court. Dismissing the reference, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate values of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. [310C] 2. The computation of the gross wealth of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the value date. All the assets of the assesee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accountancy or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assesses. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valued date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane we refer to the value Of the rights In that property. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets. [311D E] 3. The reasons for defining the valuation day in terms of the last day of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The system of assessment, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets Of the assessee. That appears plainly from the definition or "net Wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value".

The respondent, a Time Keeper in the Department of preparing pay bills and other bills of work charg ing under the Punjab Government Servants (Conduct) Rules 1966, was appointed as Inquiry Officer. The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respondent. In the inquiry report, the Inquiry Officer found that he had entered the name of Ashok Kumar in the pay roll for May 1969 and that he was a member of the staff of the Department. He also found him guilty of entering the name in the service register for May 1970 or that it was his duty to prepare the list. The respondent filed an appeal before the Central Administrative Tribunal, which dismissed the same on the ground that the punishment awarded to him was disproportionate to the delinquency of the respondent and was in stark contrast to the punishment imposed upon him. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the respondent had entered into the name o f Ashok Kumar as his own brother and that there were others too, and as such he should not be allowed to take advantage of the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority on the basis of some of the findings of the Inquiry officer; (ii) the Tribunal was wrong in directing the Governor of Orissa to reconsider the penalty awarded to the respondent when the findings recorded as to h is misdemeanour were supported by legal evidence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has no power to interfere with the penalty on the grounds that it is not commensurate with the delinquence of the official. It is appropriate to rema nise the order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on a delinquent officer. [27C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent was not offered a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and accordingly the enquiry and consequential ord er of dismissal were found to be bad. The Tribunal had no power under section 27(1) of the Act to impose any punishment to meet the ends of justice. Where the person without enquiry is dis pute guilty, removed or reduced in rank solely on the view that he would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant, the Tribunal has jurisdiction to exercise its power of review subject to the court permitting it. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the tribunal has no pow er to substitute its own discretion for that of the authority. [28D E] 1:3 The Tribunal was in error in directing that the Governor should reconsider the matter. [29F] 2.1 In the present case, there was no doubt that the respondent did not have entered the service of the department or had been working in his Division. He was only otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants ' (Conduct ) Rules which are applicable to him. The disciplinary authority must however bear in mind that the Tribunal is just a substitute to t he civil court and High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere. [30G H] 2:2 In view of the principles to which we have call ed, the order imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot be sustained. [31A B] 2 :3 The disciplinary proceedings are not vitiated by any legal or valid reasons. The punishment imposed is too severe and it is just and proper that the penalty should be reduced in its discretion to be imposed. If there has been an enquiry, the penalty would be vitiated and the order based on such enquiry would be justified having regard to the misdemeanour established. [32B C] 2(a) In the case of proceedings under section 10 of the , the Tribunal could not substitute its decision with the findings arrived at by the Inquiry Officers or the competent authority. The adequacy of penalty unless it is malafide is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of the compete nt authority. If, however, the findings are based on evidence even if some of it is found to have been irrelevant or extraneous to the matter, the Court has power to exercise that power to re examine the penalty.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with their possession of the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2, filed a suit against the appellants for a declaration that they were lessees and for an injunction restraining the defendants (appellants) from interfering in their possession. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of any land as lessee. On appeal the High Court held that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed, the second defendant had no right to remain in possession of it. In the appeal by special leave, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the suit was barred by res judicata inasmuch as the plaintiff had not been dispossessed by an act of trespass; that the cause of action for the former suit was different from the one in which the earlier suit was pending and hence irrespective of the reliefs claimed in the subsequent suit, the latter suit was clearly barred by constructive res judicata. On behalf of defendant No 1 it was submitted that the second plaintiff had failed to establish that he was a lessee and his possession was forcibly taken sometime in the second week of June, 1968; that he had not even been dispossessed in accordance with law; that in the earlier case the question regarding the tenancy of the plaintiff as a lessee was directly involved in the first suit and hence the subsequent action on the part of the defendant No 2 was wholly barred by limitation. On the other hand it was urged on behalf the respondent that the High court had wrongly held that since the subject matters of the first two suits were directly and vitally in issue, the question whether defendant No1 was a tenant or deemed tenant was not involved in any controversy; that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff having failed to apply to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that since it was not a case of mere possession but one of dispossession, the cause for the latter Suit was clearly outside the Civil Court 's jurisdiction on account of the change in law the proper course would be to follow in spirit the procedure outlined in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1024D] 1.2 The High Courts have taken a contrary view by holding that even though the Fifth amendment came into effect from 1st July, 1962, the plaintiff has not applied to the Collector for possession on the basis of the declaration sought in the suit. It is, therefore, difficult to comprehend how the High Courts were right in concluding that the first respondent was entitled to remain a tenant in respect of the land in question. The petitioners are daily rated employees. They were classified as daily rated employee and paid the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for similar work in construction industry. The Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to them. The Corporation has also not fixed any minimum wages. The petitioners have challenged the constitutional validity of the Corporation 's action. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by Article 14 expressly guaranteed in the Constitution. The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. [667B C] 1.2 The principle is not arbitrary, irrational or discriminatory. It is based on a rational differentia which has a rational nexus with the object of the Act. The differentiation is reasonable and does not violate Article 14. [668D E] 2.1 In service jurisprudence, equality before law or equal protection is a concomitant of Article 14, but it follows naturally that equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right. This was also the view expressed in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union of India, ; at 245. [669F G] 2:2 The law relating to equal pay is not an arbitrary or discriminatory one. The equality claims of the petitioners could be allowed. [670B C; 670C] 2 :3 It may be noted that the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable for their counterparts in Government service. In the first place, even assum ing that the Petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts of the government service, the petitioners cannot enforce the right to "equal pays for equal Work". The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the trial court. The High Court acquitted accused 5 and 6 of charge No. 1 framed against them under section302 read with Section 120B I. P.C., but confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to him. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section 120B read with s.120B I P. C. could not be sustained; (ii) the evidence regarding the presence of accused 7 and 8 in the company of accused 6 and 7 was not sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused 6 was found in the Company of accused 1 and 2 at the relevant time as alleged by the prosecution before and after the murder of Malan, and (iii) the High Court erred in law in holding that the conviction could not have been sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 was not a part of the conspiracy under s. 120B IPC but was a part thereof by the evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the said accused. [785C] 2. It is the case of the prosecution that the appellant alone could have fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by him in pursuance of the criminal conspiracy under which he was charged with murder of his daughter Malan and also for the offence of murder of her husband. The evidence regarding presence of the two accused at the scene of offence before and thereafter after the commission of the murder is amply corroborated by other evidence, namely, recovery of the blood stained clothes, article 54 and the medical evidence of Dr. Suresh (P.W 31) who conducted autopsy on the body of Malvan at 4.15 p.m. on 2.1.1976. [788G H; 789A] 3.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will executed a will in 1945, bequeathing certain properties to his wife. The testator died on August 22, 1945, and after his death the appellant 's son, the respondent, filed a suit for partition of the properties between himself and his wife, claiming a declaration that the said properties were his absolute property and that he was entitled to dispose of them by a will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the testator had not established that when the will was written it was not proved that the will had been executed by her husband and that the appellant had entirely failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under the will. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the execution of the Will was not established. The evidence on record showed that the testatrix was not present when the testator signed the document and that she understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature on it when she was alive at the date of the trial. Held, further, that in deciding whether the suspicions attending the execution is proved or not, the court has to consider the evidence adduced by the parties as a whole and then decide whether the propounder must remove the suspicion from the mind of the Court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The burden of proving the existence of suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution will be on the party who alleges it and that onus was heavily upon him. In deciding whether a suspicions attend to the execution, the propounder has to prove the due and valid execution of his will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances attendant on the execution the propounder should remove the said suspicions from the hands of the court by cogent evidence.

The appellant company was carrying on business of sale and purchase of Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The goods were purchased from the appellant Company by persons other than those who ran Cinemas or for any other use. The sales tax authorities held that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast, through the projectors, on cinema screens. It was further held that these were not taxable under entry No. 4 of the first schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's appeal without taking any further evidence. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the sales tax Appellate Tribunal was wrong in holding that the main use of these are carbolic acid and not that of a self propelled vehicle capable of pulling a load; that the sale of Arca carbins is covered by the 4th entry in the first Schedule to the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] 2. The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No., 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. [562 G] 3. The word "accessory" is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses also. It is its general or predominant user which seems to determine the category in which an article will fall. The first entry in this schedule relates to "motor vehicles". The words 'parts thereto ' are used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that they are known as 'cinema are car bons ' in the market. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra pradesh High Court that the goods under consideration are covered by it. [563 G 564 A] 4.

The petitioners are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners were granted a Parwana in respect of the minor minerals known as Black Trap and Hard Murrum for purposes of mining leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals. The State Government issued a notification on June 18, 1981 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966 with effect from 1 7 1985 substituting the original rule 21 of the Rules by new Rule 21. The original rule was substituted by new rule 21 by new r. 21. In the meantime, the State Government made a further amendment to the Rules in 1981 which provided that a holder of a Parished mineral granted under these rules shall pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the rate applicable to the grant of the royalty specified in the said Schedule. The amended rule 21 was substituted as Rule 21 by the new r, 21. On June 18 1985 the State Legislature passed the Gujarat Minerals Rules 1966 with retrospective effect from January 1, 1985 substituting a new rule 20 for the old rule 21. By the said notification the rate was increased from Rs.4 to Rs.7 per metric tonne by amending the rules. The respondents challenged the validity of the amended Rule 21 and the vires of the said Notification on the ground that it violated Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied on the extracted mineral was in the nature of a tax and it was not in the form of a fee which could be used only for specific purposes; that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution the State legislature had no power to make any discrimination between the two classes of persons. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the levy in question was unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The minerals belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [412C] In the instant case, the petitioners are lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes other than those which are affected by any law or rule and that the amount of royalty is ultimately passed on to the consumers. Under clause 1 of the proviso to the impugned Rule 21 a holder has to make a concession in respect to quarry leases, lease hold leases or similar minerals and he cannot manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potters whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick kiln for the purpose of mining lease is entitled to any other purpose. The cess imposed on the extraction of minor mineral would impose in any way the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the constitution regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliar 's father in Manjakartha Mudaliar Community. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the succession is "regulated by usage" and therefore the office of a hereditary trustees is in the nature of property. Held, that the word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". The word " succession ' in relation thereto includes both kinds of cases: (1) succession to the office and (2) succession being specifically provided for by the founder on condition that the scheme of such succession is still in force. In the present case, the appellant had been elected as trustee by Senganatha Mudaliar Community and since then the management of the temple and was affairs was always vested in the community of the Songunatha Mudaliars and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The fact that the artificial definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 (9) would include even such cases, does not mean that there is a succession of As office to another when on the expiration of the period for which a was appointed, there is no vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy.

The prosecution case against the appellant was that he along with two others, armed with a knife and a knife, had killed one of them. The deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). He got up and saw the accused hitting him with knife. He got down and saw two persons running ahead of him. He ran to his elder brother who was sleeping near him. When he went near him, he was already dead. The appellant was declared absconder. On hearing a noise, the deceased came out and saw one person lying on the ground with knife and another with knife, and that he had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and witnessed the incident. He also saw two other persons running towards the place where the deceased was sitting. The younger brother of the deceased who was a lepered brother was running after stabbing him with a dagger. He was also seen by the deceased when he went to the scene of occurrence. He had bleeding injury on several part of his dead body. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and convicted him under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant was not reliable because he had no motive to implicate the first accused; that there has been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first and the deceased; that the High Court erred in convicting the second respondent on the sole testimony of a single witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW4 is not reliable as he was declared absent from behind. It is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence; but the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased had been only mentioning the name of accused makes it doubtful if the crowd had gathered at the place. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is certainly an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may also not have a quali fied evidence in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that there is no other assailants who arrived at the scene. [711E F] 2. The prosecution case was that the appellant along with three others attacked PW 4 and PW 5 on the same boat with knife which he had stabbed him. The first information Report was very close to the site of occurrence within about 15 minutes of the occurrence. It was also mentioned in the First Information Report that the first deceased chased the accused as the latter was running away after stabbing the appellant with knife 's knife. The second report was lodged at the Thana which is very close and the same day. There were also no blood stains on the bench where he was said to have been stabbed. It may be that these two witnesses had stated in their first information reports that the accused was only mentioning his name as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. [612E F; 710A B] 3.

The assessee firm was carrying on business in solicitors. The partnership was carried on by the partners in a firm which carried on the business of solicitors and the assessee firm paid commission to them at the rate of Re. 1 per mensem. For the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52 and 1954 55 the Income tax Officer assessed the amounts in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased Amarchand as his income under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Income Tax Act. The assessee contended that section 24 B had no application to the income received after the death of the firm and it was capital receipt and not revenue receipt. Held, that the words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" in section 24A of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1951, meant that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income was received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his death they were liable to be taxed. The words " or any tax payable under this act" in the section did not extend to income received by the deceased person before his death and it could not be said that they were income which might be deemed by fiction to have been received by him. The provisions of section 24(B) do not extend the scope of the word "assessment" to cases provided for the levy of tax on receipts by the legal representatives in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account being the previous year in which such person died. Ellis C. any income received in the year subsequent to the previous or the account year cannot be called income received under this section. Elliis C, any income which may be deemed to have accrued by the dead person and therefore they are not liable to tax in the several years of assessments. Elis C., Allo vs Commissioner of Income tax, , referred to.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All non domicile persons were appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra State Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act and the Rules on the grounds that article 16(3) of the Constitution was violated inasmuch as it conferred a power to make laws prescribing conditions for residence in a part of a State. It was further contended that the provisions of the impugned Act were ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957, is intra vires and must be struck down. Article 16(1) of Constitution does not confer a power on the Government to make law prescribing conditions as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment in the State, or Union Territory. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. Article 35(b) does not contemplate any discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. It only means that if it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as District, Taluk, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, or union territory, which words mean what they say, neither more nor less. The intention is made clear by the words 'residence within the state or Union territories ' which words means what they says, either alone or less. It follows that section 4 of the , is ultra vires and void.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted under section 51 of the said Act and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the mere fact that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. HELD : (i) The mere fact of possession, according to the appellant, did not suffice to show that the letters were secreted by him. [415 D] (ii)The mere fact, that there is even a long delay of more than three months in deliver ing a postal articles to the postal article does not mean merely that the articles had been stolen from the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. The mere circumstance that there has been even a lapse of several years in delivering the postal articles by the appellant would not be sufficient to show the nature of possession attributable to him. In such circumstances it is sufficient to point out that he must have utilised the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession, [417 G H] (iii)The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be held that he was in exclusive possession of these articles.

The appellant, who was the husband of respondent No. 2, filed a complaint against respondent No, 2 alleging that he had been abused and be laboured by respondent No 3, the Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas. The Magistrate ordered that the complaint should be treated as a petition under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to proceed with the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence in its judgment; (ii) the Magistrate had wrongly held that the application filed by respondent NO. 2 was not supported by any affidavit sworn to or a certified copy of the order, and (iii) the complaint did not contain the date of the High Courts ' stay order. HELD : The High Court should have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant had stayed proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat when no proceeding was pending before him. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120D] In the instant case, the appellant was not aware of the interim stay order passed by the High. Court. The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the High Commissioner was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him, and it was therefore, chary of finding a judicial officers guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the said order of his High Court.

The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 302, I.P.C., by the Sessions Judge, Etawah, for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the entire report dictated by him was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in rejecting the statement of the appellant as inadmissible in his evidence, because, the evidence relied upon by the High court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. HELD : (i) The conviction of the appellants under section 307 I. P.C. must be set aside and they should be sentenced to imprisonment for life. [206 B] (ii) The extra judicial confession of an accused is not normally considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June. Both on account of the temperature and on account Of the culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant 's bathing in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to have been improbable. [207 C D] (iii) The High court erred in rejecting a statement of an approver as inadmissible under section 25 of the Evidence Act. It was not stated by sub Inspector Kishan Singh, nor it was alleged that the confession made to him was false. The evidence of the approver was corroborated by the evidence of other prosecution witnesses whose testimony had been rightly accepted by the trial court. [208 E F] (iv) The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive and purchase of a sword, which has not been normally considered in the circumstances of this case. It is not necessary that such an inference should be drawn from the facts that the accused had committed the murder. The conviction was therefore bad.

The respondent No. 1, a local authority, filed an election petition challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 (No. 23 of 1956). The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the respondent No 1 was not prompt in moving the High Court and that the petitioner did not have any objection to the inclusion of his name in the electoral rolls on October 19, 1978. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that respondent No 2 had asked for a further direction to be issued to the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31, 1978, and directed the issue of notice of the petition and stay application to the Respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules. The High Court also held that the writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the period of 20 days had been fixed for entertaining claims and objections, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objection were prevented from preferring them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 3(1), the High Commission had no jurisdiction to do so. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High, prima facie, is satisfied that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue has been brought to its notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them. [497G H] 2. The powers of the Court under Article 227 of the constitution to issue any appropriate writ are discretionary and when the High/Court finds that there has not been satisfactory explanation, it is reject ed. The final electoral roll was published on November 16, 1978 and it was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 but before December 25,1978, a few days thereafter, for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under Rule 5(1). The writ petition itself was filed on December 28, 1978 for the second time that the names of 34 persons were received by the Deputy Collector and that was rejected by the authorities concerned. [498A B] 3. In view of the fact that the period mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4( 1) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication) Rules, 1963 has been adjourned twice before, it cannot be said that there was any satisfactory explanation from the petitioners for the inordinate delayed filing of the writ petitions.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1913. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913 were filed before the Registrar of Companies on or about March 31, 1953. In the general meeting and profit & loss account for the year ending March 31. 1953 the balance sheet was prepared and submitted to the Registrar on June 30, 1956. The Registrar of companies approved the balance sheets and profit of the Company as required by section 134(4) of that Act. The appellant company filed a complaint against the company under sections 32(5) and 132(3) of , which were punishable under sub section (3) Of section 220 of the Act. In its written statement the appellant contended that no general body meeting had been held and no general meeting was held and therefore the balance Sheet and profit or loss account could not be laid before a general body, and that the balancesheet and profit account had not been laid before the company at a general meeting. The High Court accepted this contention and quashed the complaint. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the holding of the annual general meeting of the companies and laying before it of the balance Sheets only after it had been placed before the general body and that in any case, the balance book and profit, account or the profit and Loss account could be laid at the general meetings; (2) the resolution passed by the company approving the balance of the accounts and profit was not a valid sanction under section 134 of the 1913 Act or section 220 Of the Act as the case may be, and (3 ) the resolution was invalid because it contravened the provisions of section 134. HELD : (1)(a) The holding of annual general meetings and the laying before them of the Balance sheet and the profit & Loss account was a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the appellant company could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their own failure to call the general bodies meeting as a defence to the prosecution. [415 B] (b) The provisions unmistakably indicate, as they appear from section 134, that if the balance books were not adopted at the General meeting before which it was laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance statement and to the copies thereto required to be filed with the Registrar. If no such statement is annexed, the requirements of section 135(2) are satisfied. [416 C] (c) The provision in section 134 cannot be complied with if it is not shown that the books were adopted at a meeting at the special general meeting or that there was any failure to comply with the requirements thereof. [414 E F] (d) The requirement of section 133(2), therefore, must be read along with section 132(1). [417 G] (e) The expression "any person" in section 135 is used in a wide sense and includes all persons who are not citizens. Section 134 lays down various requirements which are to be complied by the Company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (a) of section 132 provides that the company shall forthwith file with the registrar a copy of the list and summary, and any default therein shall make him liable for punishment under section 135. [413 G H] (f) The word "information" in the context means information which is material to be included in the expression 'information '. In other words, the expression "information relating to the company" has been used in the sense of information as defined in section 2(a). [414 A B] In the present case, there was no evidence that the appellant had any knowledge or reason to call a general public meeting and not to call general body meetings. The failure to send the general public notice as required in section 132 (1), therefore did not make him guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133.

The trial commenced on August 9, 1951, and the accused were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court. On appeal the High Court held that section 5(1) of the Act had no application to the case as it did not provide for a speedier trial but only provided for the trial by a special court and did not make any distinction between offences under section 3 and those under section 5. The State appealed to this Court with certificate. Held, that the classification made in section 5 (1) was valid and the classification must be held to be reasonable. The classification must not be arbitrary but must be based on some qualities or characteristics which are peculiar to persons or who are left out but those qualities or attributes must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The distinction between the two classes of offences is, therefore, well established and that in each case judges must look straight into the heart of things and regard the facts of each case concretely much as a jury would do; and yet not quite as a result of the enactment of the law itself. The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He was later promoted to the post of Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the Medical College. The post of Professor of radiology in the medical college was a post belonging to the Central Health Service and continued to work in that capacity till October 8, 1964. By an order dated January 1, 1965, the Government of India, Ministry of Health, Health & Family Planning Department of Health by its letter dated April 6, 1965 directed that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the said post as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality. The appellant was not only holding the post as an Associate Professor but also performing the duties attached to the teaching post of Radiologist. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated April6, 1965 and the order of the Central Government dated January 17, 1976. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the post was divided into two classes viz., Class I and Class II and the appellant was also performing his duties as an Assistant Professor of Pathology in a medical college and treated as an assistant Professor of P Associate Professor in that Department. It was further submitted that the teaching experience gained by him while holding the said posts was different and the post could not he taken into consideration for determining his eligibility for appointment as Associate Professor. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant could be considered to have been appointed to the Post of Associate professor in Ma reciprocology in Malulana Azad medical College, which had fallen vacant in 1973. As a necessary consequence, it was eligible to be considered by the Union Public Service Commission for appointment of Assistant Professor as Associate Professors of Radiological Institute in Mahammed Azad Medical college. [8E F] 1.2 The Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, New South Wales, has been using the Central Excise and Taxation Commissioner 's Office Manuals of the Government for the purpose of reorganising the service into five categories viz., Categories I, C, D, E, E and E. The said office does not make him eligible for appointment in the post. If the appellant is eligible to hold the post he can always apply irrespective of the fact whether or not he is in the line of promotion. It is for the Union Government to advertise the post in the manner provided by r. That being so, the appellant who was a highly qualified person and has the requisite teaching experience, as Radiologist cum Associate Professor, of Radiology (ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital, could be appointed by direct recruitment from amongst persons holding the posts of Associate Professors or Assistant Professor in any medical college or teaching institution from Grade I and Grade II. [88G H; 89A] 2.1 It is not for the Court to give the appellant promotion or make his appointment to a post of Assistant Director of Radiologists in Mahammad Azad Medical Colleges. The Ministry 's letter dated January 25, 1982 addressed to the Secretary (Medical), Delhi Administration that the said office of Professor in Manaecology (Ex officio) will be abolished with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into account. It may be pointed out that the Ministry of Education has been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maulana Nehru Medical College for the Municiological Department of studies for the academic year 1966 65. [89F G] 2:2 The appellant, while holding a non teaching post in a teaching hospital like the Irin Azad Medical Institute, was not holding the Post as an associate Professor ofika Radiology and he had the requisite research experience as Radiologists cum Associate Professors in the said institution.

The appellant company had taken on lease a piece of land for the purpose of manufacturing tea. The workmen were paid minimum wages and this was covered by item 2 of the Schedule attached to the Order of reference. The Company made an application under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was no identical industry in the region comparable with the company and therefore, the workmen were entitled to bonus on any further rise in price index. On appeal by the workmen it was contended before this Court that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in not making calculation of surplus available on the basis of the Full Bench Formula approved by this Court in French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs The Workmen, ; , and that the principle laid down by this court in French Motors (India) Ltd. case was applicable to the present case. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had not committed any error of fact or law requiring interference by this tribunal. [674 E] In the instant case, the Tribunal committed an apparent error in arriving at its decision and consequently the total minimum wage packet of a workman in the company should be fixed at Rs. 95. This was done on the assumption that the minimum wage fixed by the appellant company was not uniform throughout the period of 5 years. [678 F] (ii) The finding of fact recorded by the Industrial Tribunal is correct and must be upheld. [677 G H] French Motor car Co. vs Its Workmen, , referred to. (iii) The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed as that year was still running when the award was given by the tribunal on the 11th January, 1964. [676 G] (iv) The appellant company is paying profit bonus equivalent to three months ' basic wage of each workman.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer, Ward A, after making certain deductions from his income assessed the appellant under section 147 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The appellant challenged the validity of the notice on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act and that the assessment order was invalid because it did riot comply with section 151 (2). HELD: The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. [447 D] The report of the Income Tax Officer to the commissioner showed that he had taken into account the various amounts which were mentioned in those communications. All that he said was that from those communications "it appears that these persons (alleged creditors) are name lenders and the transactions are bogus". He has not even come to a prima facie conclusion that the transactions to which he referred are not genuine transactions. He is not satisfied that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice under section 148. [449 E] The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that the transaction to which the appellant referred were not genuine. He could not have issued a notice tinder section 148, and therefore he could not be said to have issued any notice under s 148. Further his report mentions "Hence proper investigation regarding these loans is necessary".

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calicut, was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Income tax Officer held that the business of the assessee was carried on by two independent firms, namely, M/s. B. & Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Mer chants, Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., and that it was succeeded by a company as owner of the business in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25(4) could be claimed. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also the Tribunal held against the appellant on appeal to this Court. It was contended for the appellant that (1) the firm had been dissolved in 1937 and the family became entitled to relief under section 25 (4) of the Income tax Act, 1922; (2) the business must have been carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, that the family was not carrying on any business at the time when the firm succeeded, and (3) the family had no right to the benefit under section 26(4). HELD: The appeal must be allowed. (i) The firm carried on a business in Calcutta and Bombay and its business was carried out by two separate firms. The partners constituting the appellant at the moment of the transfer in 1948 were not carrying any business in existence but were merely a change in the constitution of a partnership which had been assessed to tax under the Indian income tax Act of 1918, and therefore, the family could not be said to have been dissolved on April 1, 1939. [117 E] (ii) The family was entitled to the benefits of section 26 (4). It is possible that there may be a succession only to the business which had paid tax under that provision while the emphasis in sub section (3), on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carrying on an earlier firm, was that the person succeeding should have succeeded his predecessor in carrying on the business as a whole.

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The appellant 's case was that the suit properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband and his two sons. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties belonged exclusively to the respondent and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th undivided share. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to joint family; (2) the respondent had effected partition of the suit house between himself and his brothers; (3) the appellant 'S 's 1/24 share in the joint Hindu Family properties was only 1/25th, that the respondent 's father had effected a partition of that house by metes and bounds during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s interest upon his death; (4) the plaintiff 's share in her own property was only one half and that therefore, by reason of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, the pre conditions of section six were satisfied. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The suit properties belong to joint Hindu family and are self acquisitions. [766D] (b) The respondent 'S had effected the partition of his coparcenary property by metes & bounds during his life time between him and his sons. [764B C] (c) The appellant had a share in a joint family property, the fourth being, Khandappa 's wife 's husband '. The proviso to section 6 states that the decision of the appeal must turn on the meaning to be given to Explanation 1 of section6. [774C D] (d) The proviso does not provide further that in the circumstances of a case where there is no partition between the plaintiff and his son, the property should be deemed to have been allotted to him if a partition was effected between her husband & his two brothers. [754D E] (e) The Explanation to section six states that "the proviso shall not apply to a partition in respect of the joint Family property". The Explanation does not say that the share of the heirs must be ascertained on the basis that they bad separated from one another and had received a share therein during the life time of the deceased. [754F G] (f) The expression "the widow ' shall be deemed not to have received in the notional partition. The Explanation applies only to cases where there are two or more persons, who are relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and not as a limited owner. [758G H] (g) The explanation does not mean that the heirs should receive the property equal to that of a son. The expression 'the widow shall be "to have failed to furnish a return of his income". The proviso is intended to be explanatory of the provision for determining the share in property itself. It has to be read as the whole and the very first step, to ascertain the share, which the deceased had in the coparcenary property because after all, the plaintiff has a 1/4th interest in that share. [759A B] (2)(a) In the instant case, the respondent was not entitled to demand partition yet, if a partial partition took place between the appellant and his brother, the respondents would be entitled to receive a share equal to the appellant or her share in their interest. [761B C]. (b). The High Court was right in holding that section 6 did not provide for a rerograde step to determine the share. while section 6 does not prescribe any further procedure. [763C D].

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were framed by the Central Government under section 11(2) of the Life Insurance Act, 1956. The regulations provided that an employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age but the appointing authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the corporation to do so direct such employee to retire on completing 58 years. The respondent was a member of the Employees State Insurance Corporation and was appointed to service of that Corporation on 1st Sept., 1956. In the year 1965 there were more than 200 insur ities carrying on life insurance business in India. After the coming into force of the Act, the Life Insur ive Corporation of lndia (Staff), Regulations, 1961, framed under section ll(2)(b) of Act, read with the settlement entered into between the respondent and its employees on or about 1st October, 1956, was abolished by the Life Assis tration Corporation. The appellant Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations were not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of the respondent Corporation under section l9(2), and that the Regulations were not applicable to them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had the right to continue in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age of 60 years, he could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regulations are applicable to all employees belonging to class lI and II of the Corpora tion. They are applicable even to those who joined the service after 1 st September 1956. [196B] 2. Regulation 19 is not violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is only in 1965 under the settlement that the age was fixed at 60 years. In order to get over this difficulty, it is necessary to have a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be attained thereby. The Act itself made a distinction between transferred employees and those recruited to the Service of the State on or before 1st April 1956. It does not make any difference whether the employees who were appointed prior to 1st August 1956 were transferred to any service of tho Corporation on that date. [197D E] 3. The High Courts erred in striking down regulation 19(1) as amended in 1977 and in directing the Corporation to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed the age Of 60 years.[197F] 4. Regulation 20(2 ) is not repugnant to Article 14 of the Constitu tion. It only provides for a reasonable nexus between transfer of employees and their transfer to the Corporation. [198G] 5. The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 are applicable in respect of the transferred employee and those who entered the service prior to that date by the Corporation in respect thereof. [199B] 6. The Central Government services and the State Government services are governed by the Act itself. It may be so.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India stating that the Judge had been given an impression that he was not a Judge but a politician who had come to Barwani in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The letter stated that the Judges of the Bar Association were very poor and that they had failed miserably in all fields. The appellants took a copy of their letter to this Chief Minister, who was present at the hearing. They also wrote a note stating that if in view of this Hon 'ble Court the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by them and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the letter did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The letter in the instant case was addressed by the deponent to the Governor of Punjab with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon ' blemis sion of a Judge or this Court should steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters. [245E] 1.2 In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communication in question was brought personally by two members of the bar association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a open cover addressed by one of the members of Bar Association, Bhiwni to Chandigarh. The deponent further stated that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Honble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. [246G H] 1:3. The contents of the letter were not disputed and challenged. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. In order that the action may be taken for any reasons contempt of Court, one would he more swer than the affidavit himself. Therefore, the deponent tender his apology to this Hon`ble Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. [243A B] 1 :4. The matter did not constitute any contempt. The contempt proceedings were dropped.

The petitioner, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. During the investigation of that case the Income tax Officer found that the petitioner had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thereby evaded tax. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the grounds (i) that the provisions of section 6(4) Of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution, (ii) that there was no substantial difference in the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner 's income and did not affect his liability to pay income tax. Held, that the procedure for reference under section 5 (1) Of section 5 Of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure provided under the Act in respect of assessment or reassessment proceedings taken under the provisions thereof by themselves form a class distinct from those who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act. The procedure prescribed in this matter by the Act was substantially prejudicial and the persons against whom proceedings were taken under section 6 (4) were deprived of the rights of appeal, second appeal and revision conferred by sections 31, 32 and 33 Of the Income Tax Act. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the impugned provisions of the impugned section are discriminatory and unenforceable. The provisions of article 20(3) of India Constitution do not offend against article 14 Of the Constitution and are therefore void and unenforceable under article 14.

In the year 1963, the appellant company filed an application for prosecution of its Secretary, the Federation, under the . On receipt of the report, the Registrar of Shops & Establishments, New Delhi, issued a notice to the Federation calling upon it to register the establishment 'and submit its objections. The Union filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated February 4, 1964 passed by the Chief Inspector. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activity of the appellant was a " commercial establishment" within the definition of "commercial establishment". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the activities of the Association were not a "business or trade" within section 2, (5) the application of the provisions of the . was not maintainable; and (ii) even if the activity was a ' commercial establishment ', the words "any business, business or profession" given in the Act would not take it out of the definition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his heirs. The income tax authorities assessed the appellant to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50 under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The question was whether on a true interpretation of cl. (viii) of section 4 of the indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1950, the sum of Rs. 36,396/ received by the assessee as an allowance during the previous year of assessment was revenue income liable to tax under the said Act. The High Court answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the right which was conferred on the assessee was not a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment, and that the source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collection from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee 's predecessor in interest was agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. HELD: (i) The right which is conferred on an assessee by cl. 3 of the deed of lease is not a "agricultural income" as defined in section 2 of the Indian income tax Act. [707 B] Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa vs Raja Bahadur Kamakhaya Narayan Singh and Ors., ; , followed. (ii) The source of payment of pension was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined by section 2 (1)(c). [708 C D] (iii) The amount which had been received by an assessee as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income was received, it is neither income exempt under section 4(3)(viii) nor revenue income. Therefore, the allowance was revenue receipt and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [070 F G] Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Bihar & Orissa vs Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, ; , referred to. (iv) The allowance is revenue income and not exempted from taxation. [700 C D]. Commissioner of Incometax, Bihar, Patna vs Kunwar Sri Trivendayala Sir Kameshwar Singh, I.L.R. , approved.

The appellants of Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 claimed to have been appointed as Supervisors Gra de 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966 a nd had filed these writ petitions claiming that the same relief may be granted to them also as was granted by this Court to 75 appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 441/81. The three civil miscellaneous petitions referred to above on the other hand have been made by the appel lants of Civil Appeals No.441 of 1981 asserting that the direction given by this court on 2nd February, 1981 has not been complied with in t he manner as it ought to have be en by the respondents and they should be accordingly required to comply with the said direc tion.
