The Karnataka State Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the vires of section 63(7) of the . The High Court set aside the grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63 (7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the proviso, and that the grant was set aside. The High court also took the same view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of some of the private operators that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that in the case of the court interpreted the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State Road transport Corporation would have a monopoly. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Motor Vehicles Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. The proviso to Section 47(I H) for example, provides that in case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matters of stage carriage permit. [1015C D] 2. Clause (iv) of section 47 (1 H), for example provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriage permits from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given priority over applications from individual owners. [ 1015E] 3. The word 'repreference" in section 2(25) is unconstitutional and it is not necessary that the department is able to exercise some control on the functioning of these operators. [10F] 4. Clause(iv) provides for a preference, not to operators of tourist vehicles but to operators or of tourist cars and travel agents. Though the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles, the preference is confined to operators who of tourist car and travel agent. Although the permits are for Tourist vehicles, it mentions that approval carries with it certain privileges, such as allotment of ex STC vehicles and that it is, therefore, necessary that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the car hire business or that they must be ex Defence Service personnel, who satisfy certain prescribed conditions. The matter appears to have been left to the total discretion of the Central Government, virtually as we said, pre empting the decision. [1005C E] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 's contention was that the transaction was a sale of goods which were discontinued or the ownership of which had changed. The appellant contended that the State Government had no authority under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the, business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in his hands. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Rule 21A is ultra vires as it does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee; and (ii) Rule 22(c) is ultra rites. HELD: The rule making powers of the state Government under section 9 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 are beyond the rule made by the State Legislature either under section 10 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., ; , followed. Badrida Chetty vs C .I. T., ; and Badridah vs C I.T. (Central), Calcutta, ; , referred to.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (2). On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the order and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, he contended that the High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311 as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy thereof. Held, that the appellant was entitled under the Workmen 's Compensation Act, 1906 to compensation from the shipowners not only in respect of his wages but also of the retainer, which must be taken into account as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. The liability to pay salary when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay wages. In the present case, the liability to payment of arrears of pay was not a liability arising out of any contract but was a liability in respect Of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. The decree of the High court decreeing payment of wages was truly a liability and it could not be said that the Government servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of report of Enquiry Officer. State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. Held further, that in the present ease, the appellant had failed to prove that he had been given reasonable opportunity within the meaning of article 313(2). The High Court was right in holding, that there was a breach on his part and that the refusal by the competent officer to provide him with a copies of the reports of the enquiry held against him amounted to violation of article 14.

The appellants were the owners of a coal mine. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the said land on the allegation that the appellant had encroached upon it and had rendered the remaining coal liable to be removed under the previous lease in favour of the appellants. The trial court held that the respondent had encroached on the land and passed an order for the value thereof by way of damages. On appeal, the High Court accepted the finding of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts in India had wrongly decided the question whether the respondents had knowledge of the trespass only within three years of the suit and not within three year in the circumstances of the case, and that the finding was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the onus of proving the knowledge of his father wag on the respondents to prove that he had knowledge about the encroachment only within 3 years of his coming into possession and that it was not permissible for a court to reconstruct the plan with reference to revenue records when the plan is self contained and drawn to scale. [501 D] (ii) The onus of proof in the former sense is on the party who comes to Court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. In the present case, the burden was upon the appellant to prove the fact that the knowledge was within three yea years of its purchase and not beyond three years. [500 E] (iii) The burden of proving that the information given by the respondents was false lies on the plaintiff who asserts a right and it may be having regard to the circumstances, of each case, that the facts proved were not in his knowledge or belief. [50 F G] Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, Pat. 75 I.A. 206, referred to. (iv) The presumption under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act is a rebuttable one and the onus is upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove affirmatively that he has the knowledge or knowledge of it. [51 F G]. Talykshan vs Gimmajanta, Pat, 75 I A.C.

The appellant was a crosscutter. It was alleged that the Secretary of the appellant had been suspended and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of grave indiscipline and misconduct. The appellant replied that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. The same day, the appellant informed the same day that in view of his denial, a departmental enquiry was held and he was also placed under suspension pending inquiry. The Industrial Tribunal found that something appeared to have happened on the afternoon of June 21, 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant could not be said to have taken disciplinary action against him for misconduct. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the employer could defend the action under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without giving any reason and therefore its action could not stand on a different footing as in the present case. The Tribunal had rightly held that there was nothing more to be said and that the industrial court could inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(b). The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of power in this case was bona fide and was not colourable. The fact that the enquiry was not held by the appellant and action was taken under r 18(c) did not make any difference. The industrial court had the right to inquire into whether there was a cause that might be sufficient or not and therefore having failed to justify its action must suffer the consequences.

The appellant was the receiver of a theatre belonging to the respondent. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that as sub lessee or licensee under law it was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the cinema, and that the respondents were estopped from denying its rights to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [445 B] (ii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has recorded a finding that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease and that it was not even averred that it had been a lease. The High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court and which could not be decided by the High court until the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. [441 G H] (iii) The High court has recorded findings that the appellant was entitled under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 to obtain an order for exhibiting exhibit motion picture in the cinema theatre under the agreement. [442 C D] (iv) The trial Court had not decided any issues at all. It had also held that the question asked in cross examined by the appellant did not decide any issue at that stage. The Trial Judge was therefore right in holding that the questions asked were already concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. [443 D E] (v) The order passed by the trial Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was found unfit by an order dated 31st March, 1983. He was invalided from I.A.F.I.L. and was discharged on 30th August, 1985. The said term was extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The respondent filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging his termination order contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th of August,1985 or not unless there were a further exten sion. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to be dismissed. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order of termination was an invalid one since it had been issued on the basis of Vigilance Report and no opportunity had been given to the respondent to show cause why such action should not be taken against him. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has while setting aside the order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent was entitled for salary upto 30th September, 1985 unless there is a further Extension. [243D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the High court that the Order of termination issued in his case was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th October, 1985 were liable to he ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. [244E] 1:3. The order passed on review was wholly unsustainable. [245F] 2.1 In the penultimate paragraph of the judgment dated 24.3.1988 it is stated that the High COurt had while setting out the Vigilance Report, considered the Vigilance report and no further extension of service. If the respondent were really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24 3 1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not done.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not reliable, conflicting and improbable. HELD: (1) The discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the Sessions Judge. The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The witnesses were not able to identify if they saw the accused making a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased. The distance between the two places to the place of occurrence was 6 miles. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side. According to the prosecution, the victim received an incised wound in his hand and that the doctor who examined him found several abrasions and contusions on the person of the accused. The plea of the appellant that he had no deep motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the occurrence was not accepted by the High Court. [368 D E] (2) The discrepancy in the statement of the doctor was of a major nature and it could have been explained by the prosecution. It was obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [369 G] Sheo Swarup vs State of U.P., ; , applied. Sheo Swarup 's case, referred to. (3) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. R. Fantle reported in (5) Salmon J. in Khem Karan & Ors. vs State, A.I.R. 1970 S.C. 1423, applied.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that (i) the President of India could not be removed from his office unless and until he had been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed removal; (ii) the provisions of section 6(1) (c) were not applicable to the case of a Judge who was not a member of the Higher Judicial Service; (iii) the High Court was in error in holding that the President could be removed only by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament in the manner provided in Article 124(4); and (iv) the power to punish a Judge under section 6 of the Act was very wide enough to include Judges of the High Courts as well as Judges of other High Courts. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The President is given the power of appointment and promotion of a judge of the highest Civil Court as well. [297G] 1.2 The President of the India could be treated as the competent authority to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of the high Courts. The President, therefore, being the authority competent to appoint and to remove him from his duties, must be deemed to have been the competent Authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a person who holds such an office. [298B] 1:3. The word "office" in section 6 (1) of Act is wide enough not to include judges of the higher judiciary but also for the other offences under clauses 4 and 5 of Article 124. [299D] 1 :4. The expression "office", in clause (c), has to be read as a part of the scheme of the Constitution, which includes the office of Chief Justice of a High Court. [300E F] 1I2. The words "office or office" in clause 2(a) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authori ty under section 4 of the . [300F G] 1l3. In other words, if the holder of a public office during his tenure in office cannot be prosecuted without sanction under section six(1), it will follow that he will be immune from prosecution not only under section 161 but also under section 165 of the Indian Penal Code. [301B C] 1 4.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were members of a Saha caste, a Scheduled Caste. Abhait was a sub caste. The appellant challenged the election of Abhiman on various grounds including the ground that Abhoys had not belong to the sub caste specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant did not belong either to the Scheduled Caste or to any Schedule Tribe and therefore, he was not a member belonging to the Schedule Caste specified in Item 40. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Abhaits were originally belonged to the Sunri caste but for a long time past they had formed themselves into a different caste which had no connection with the Suniti caste and therefore did not fall within the Sunti caste. HELD: (i) The order of the High Court is set aside and the election petition dismissed. [390 B] (ii)The appellant must be held to belong to a Scheduled Tribe specified in items 40, 41 and 42 for he said "these Sahas" within the meaning of Item 40 of that Schedule. It is legitimate to think that if the excluded Sahas were those Suniti by caste, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Saha 's name is a Scheduled caste, the word "Care" in the expression "excluding Saha" in item 41 must, without more. also refer to a caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunri Caste. [391 C D] (iii) The appellant was not entitled to succeed on the ground of his being a member in the Saha ' caste specified by item 40.

The appellant was convicted under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant had demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 for the furniture and the motor garage in question from the respondent No. 1 and that the latter paid him Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs, 2,000 was paid to be paid to the appellant. The appellant pleaded that he had been in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence and that he was also to be a caretaker of his flat and as such could not pay the rent directly to the respondent. Held, that the word "relinquishment" used in section 19(1)(a) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, LVII of 1947, is not a term of art and was intended to convey or indicate an assignment of the tenancy and not a relinquishment of his tenancy by the tenant. The words "the relinquishment of tenancy of any premises" in section 18 are wide enough to include the transfer by a tenant of his interest which he has in the lessor. The word "distin quently" does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing.

The appellant company was a partnership firm. It functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry. The workmen were members of the Tata Consultancy Engineers ' Association. They served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted they filed an application before the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication under section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The claim of the Union was resisted by the appellant who maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. The Tribunal held that the new scale of pay had been fixed in accordance with the recommendations of the Fourth Pay Commission and that there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of basic wage. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the Tribunal had not considered the range of permissible retrospectivity and that the financial capacity as the Tribunal observed was very much more than plain and plain that the increase in the dearness allowance and house rent allowance could be justified only if the demand of the company was accepted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of basic wages, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capaci ty of the appellant. [176F G] 2. The financial capacity, as the tribunal observed, constituted one of the principles which are required to be followed in fixing the wage structure. It is not necessary that the wage scales should be revised in every case. The basic idea underlying the award is to give a flat increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised pay scales and other awarded reliefs. [177G H] 3. The Industrial Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode and it is not disposed of on merits. It has given cogent reasons for adopt a different method. [178A B] 4. The tribunal was wrong in giving a different scale to the appellant company. The order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal is set aside and the Tribunal directed that the pay scales of different categories should be fixed with flat increase in each category. [179C D] 5. The additional financial capacity of the workmen would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Industrial Tribu nal thought that an all round flat increase should be made in every flat cum industry cum industry. It did not give any ad hoc increase of salary, and therefore, it took a different view. [180F G; 181A] 6. The appellant company is directed to pay the additional dearness allowance to each of its employees in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. [181B] 7. The payment of dearness allowances to each employee should also be made with reference to the basic wage scales pertaining to different categories. The revised wage scale had necessarily to commence with figures Rs.150/ in that category. The revision of the wage scale was necessitated by a change in the basic pay structure. [182C] 8. The new scale had, therefore, to commence from December 22. 1978 and it would be necessary for the workmen to fitted into the revised scales of pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they surely would be much concerned with immediate benefits which may be due to the immediate benefit according to their That was what the Industrial Tribunals had found in making the award dated December 20, 1978. [183E F] 9.

The respondent, an award made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award, and in spite of the Award, the appellant paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The Tribunal held that section 2(vi) included wages fixed by an award in an industrial dispute between the employer and his employees and that the refusal of the employer to pay to them wages at the rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the respondents the said prescribed wages. The High Court affirmed this finding of the Tribunal. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 2 (vi) are applicable only to the wages fixed under the award but not to the workmen. [417 B] (ii) The terms in question need not be express and can be implied; but they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment and since an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. [420 C] (iii) The fact that on references made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have invariably been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore, the basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad that section was not applicable to the case because the wages prescribed by an Award could not be included within the definition prescribed by section 2 of the , before it was amended in 1958. [416 D E] (iv) The effect of construing the unamended definition of wages is that the old wage structure became inoperative and the place is take by the wages structure prescribed under the Award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties because that, in truth, is the effect of industrial adjudication. [414 E F] (v) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended section 2. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that, on references by the Industrial Tribunal, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribe by the Award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of Act before it is amended.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was charged with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which he had taken to his residence and misappropriated them. The trial court convicted him under section 465, Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 409 of the Indian Penal code for criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51 shown as paid to him for his wages. On appeal by the State Government the High Court held that proof that the thumb impressions in the acquittance roll were that of the appellant was sufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate court. The State appealed to this Court with certificate granted by the High Courts. It was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parama and that therefore no sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be taken against him. Held, that the conviction of the respondent was illegal as sanction under s. 197(I) of Code of criminal procedure was necessary for prosecuting a public servant under section409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the appellant had been acquitted by the Trial Court did not affect his conviction. The sanction under S. 197 (1) was required only in cases where the official character of the person giving the information was found to be irrelevant or extraneous. The mere fact that a public officer was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime, would not make him liable for prosecution under section 196(1). Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1948 Pat. 75, approved.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. The main argument was confined to the question whether business losses incurred outside Travancore State could be set off against income under another head, the taxability of income arising from each head being separate. Held, that the words " profits or gains" used in section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act of 1918 were " a loss of profits or gain ". The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. There it was held that section 10 Of the Indian Act had to be read with section 14(2)(e) and if profits could not be added for the purposes of total income " losses sustained also could not he deducted. Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Madras, ; , followed. The mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be set aside against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict that scope of the proviso to the profits and loss losses arising in Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10. Arunachalanam Chettiar Chettiar vs C. A. No. 259/58, relied on. The word " profit " is used in the first part of the definition of total world income " and chargeability of total profits under section 3 or the provisions of section 4 where in the case of a resident total income includes income, profits and gain accruing within or without British India or in any Indian State or British India, these losses could not by virtue of the Explanation be deducted from profits made in British India. Arunachalukam Chettiar 's Case, , distinguished.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company. The respondent company was converted into a Public Limited Company and the Head Office of the Company was at Calcutta. In July 1947, the Company took over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. On the question whether it should be fixed at 58 or at 60, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that the age of retirement should be 58 and not 60. [426 B] (ii)The Tribunal was right in holding that the date of retirement of the appellant workmen should be the 58 or 60 years in view of the fact that the company had been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 60 years, and that the Company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age. [427 C] Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , followed. (iii)The question whether the concern should be fix at 58 was a matter which was not raised before this Court in the present case. The Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it has ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend is established in fact. [ 428 D] Dunnop Rubber Company Ltd., V. Workmen, , referred to. (iv)The award of the Tribunal was not challenged before this court. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 58 years and that it had taken some more time in the region for doing so. The appellant company did not dispute that the figures given by the various concerns were correct.

The first respondent company was incorporated in 1961 and its incorporation in the year 1961. The Board of Directors of the Company passed a resolution on May 19, 1965 to sell certain shares of the company to the first respondent. On June 4, 1965 the first appellant issued an order under section 237(b) of the appointing 4 persons as inspectors for investigating the affairs of the respondent company and also appointed one of them as Inspectors for investigation into the affairs. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that the Board had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the power conferred on the Chairman by section 237 (b) was administrative and not judicial. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the powers conferred on him by section 236(b), were exercised only to make what was implicit in section 10E(5) read with section 642(1) clear and that the distribution of the work of the Board being merely a matter of procedure, the order of the Chairman transferring the functions under section 9(b)(i) to himself did not amount to sub delegation of the power of the board. HELD : (i) The power conferred by section 235(b). is administrative in character and not administrative. [334 B] (ii) The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and circumstances which indicate that the business of the first company was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other persons or persons. It is only when such a power is conferred by statute that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Boards. [330 C] (iii) The Board has no power to delegate its function under section 236 to itself and therefore the order passed by the first appel lant is invalid. [328 D] (iv) The order made by the Board is not invalid because it was made by a Chairman of a Board. It was not challenged in any court.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The conviction was correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. It is legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. [724 D E] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market and they have been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. The time gap is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 E F] In this case, there was no other evidence in the present ease which points to the complicity of the 14 appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they cannot be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn is one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity.

The petitioners, who were carrying on business in poisons, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (which was enacted as a Central enactment) and section 5 of that Act. Dismissing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The provisions of neither section 2 nor 5 are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [222D] 2.1 No comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it is intended to control over the traffic in poison. It states that the State Government may by rule regulate the import, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances which are used for purposes mentioned therein can certainly be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. [223E] 2:2 The provisions contained in Section 2(3) of Act, impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as poison and that the same is left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison for the purpose of the . [222F G] 2 :3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as an poison for sale and the sale of the specified poison. It is in exercise o this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old rule by following Rule 12. [224H;225A B] 2 .4. The Notification and its applica tion to any areas would depend upon the necessity for declaring the substance, as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lute the possession and sell of the same. It was not all poisonous substances that were brought within the regula tions under the . The notification did not contain any such guidelines when it was amended. [225B C] 2 5. The provision of neither Section 2 nor the impugned notification are hit either by any con tentional limitation or any infirmity. The writ petition accordingly fails and is dismissed.

The appellants were partners of a firm styled "Bhojaji Sobhachand" carrying on business at Madras as importers of yam and also as agents and adathias. Sobhachand, one of the partners of Bhojaji Sobha Chand with 16% share in the profit and loss was the father of Seshmal, Ramniklal and Lakshmichand, partners of the appellants. In the books of account of the appellant which were main tained according to the mercantile system there was a current sarafi account in respect of their transactions with the Bombay firm in which were credited the funds transmitted from Bombay in respect thereof. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as chemists and druggists nor in the Course of their money lending business. He held that the debts did not fall within section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the amount of Rs. 2,68,385 written off by the assessee in their books of accounts as irrecoverable was not one incurred in the way of money lending or for any other purpose as preferred to para 7 above. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but in appeal the Tribunal held that on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in disallowing a sum of Rs 2, 68,385/ written off as irrecoverable. On further appeal by the Department to the High Court it was contended that there were three important circumstances which appear from the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Income tax officer from which it may be inferred that the advances made by the appellants to the Bombay firms were not in respect Of loans in the ordinary course of money lent business of the asses see. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that there was no question of "locating any portion thereof as between the business of money lenders or for anything other purpose" as preferred ' to para. 7 above, and therefore the amount was allowable under section 10 (2) (xi). On appeal by special leave: Held, that before the question may be answered it is necessary to call for a supplementary statement of the Case from the Tribunal. The statement submitted by the Tribunal is also inadequate. It contains only a summary of the business relations between the appellants and the Bombay Firm, a statement as to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, the interest if any charged and a summary or summary of orders made by Income tax Officers, the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner and the Tribunal, and the High Courts. The statements submitted by tile Tribunal are also inadequate and it contains only summary of business relations. It is true as contended by the learned Counsel for the Revenue that the conclusions reached by the tribunal are not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. It cannot be denied that the findings reached by tho Tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. The tribunal has found that the monies sent by the appellant to the Madras firm were not loans made in the normal course of its money lending trade, nor in respect o any other business of assessee. As this is the finding with regard to the whole of the amount it cannot be deny that the finding reached by tile tribunal are findings Of fact and these findings are based on evidence on the record.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners filed petitions in this Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that they had not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act. This Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the petitioners that as the awards in these cases have not been made within one year from September 20, 1984, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed and therefore, they were not entitled to be made within three years from the date of publication of the declaration. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these special leave petitions. [565E] 2. The facts of the case are highly material and there is no reference in the Special leave petitions to any to the stay order and it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material. [566F] 3. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time was a matter of direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. If he fails to do so, and suppresses material facts his application is liable to be dismissed. [567G H] 4. The High Court granted stay of the further proceedings. Whatever the ultimate effect of the order was highly important in the deter mination of these Special Leave petitions, it cannot be rejected on the grounds that the non production of the very same certainly amount to suppression. [568A B] 5. If the respondents fail to do any thing and suppress material facts, his application was liable to he dismissed. The special leave Petitions are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1953 with the object of securing basic pay on January 1, 1962. The first group consisted of workmen who were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of pay applicable to them under the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal decision dated April 1, 1965. In the second group there were workmen who entered service of the bank before 31st January, 1959 and were paid dearness allowance on the basis that they would be fitted in the new scales of pay provided by the Sastry Award as modified from time to time. The appellant company claimed that the workmen would be entitled to increments as provided under the Desai award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para 5.356 of the Sastry awards as modified and were not entitled to increment in the revised scale. The Labour Appellate Tribu nal held that the adjustment basic pay was to be fixed on January 31, 1959, and that the adjusted basic pay in the old scale would draw basic pay from January 1. 1962 and thereafter they would he fitted in new scales with effect from January l, 1959. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that the adjusting basic pay had to be taken as on January l. 1959 and not on January I, 1959; that the adjustments were made in accordance with cl. (ii) of para 292 of the Desai Award as amended by the award as amended and that they were only entitled to those benefits which were given to workmen or the maximum in the existing scale of the pay provided for by the said Sastry Award. HELD: The adjustment basic salary in cl. 5.3 of the award was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January Ist, 1962 and therefore when cl. 2(a) speaks of adjusted basic wage it must refer to the same date as in cl.(iv) which provides for actual calculations starts with the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii)" and therefore the actual calculation made under el. (iv) must be subject to clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). [903 D E] The adjustment in cl, 5. 3(a)(1) has to be calculated as on 1st January 1959.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel in Calcutta, challenged the grant of four acres of land out of Begumbari Compound to India Hotel Co. The High Court held that the decision to lease the Begumbar land to the Taj Group of Hotels was taken on February 12, 1981 and that it was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the Zoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters, there would still remain sufficient land for accommodating the existing facilities. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the decision of the High Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the second Cabinet Memorandum dated September 9, 1981 on which date the Government took the final decision to grant the lease made no mention of the needs and interests of the Zooo or the facilities provided in the Begambari land for the Zoological Garden and there was no way by which the Government could divest the ZOogical Garden of the land except by a procedure known to law such as acquisition or requisition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burial ground for rubbish. [260F] 1.2 In the face of all these material facts, it cannot be seriously contended that there was an infinite variety of coniderations which may have to be taken into account by the Government in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Govern ment in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest. [262G H] 1:3 The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act have no relevance to the question of the power of the government to transfer the Begumberland land to a Taj Group o f Hotels. The Chief Minister 's attention was expressly drawn to the Managing Committee 's first Resolution expressing its opposition to the proposal to give the land for construction of a Five Star Hotel on the Begangumbari land as a final decision, to the hotel group to start a Five star hotel, which according to the Government was a prime need to the city of Calcutta. The next question is whether the Government of West Bengal acted with probity in not inviting tenders or in not holding a public auction but negotiating straightaway at arm 's length with the Taj group of Hotels. [263A B] 1 :4 The provisions Of the BengalPublic Parks Act, 1904 have no relevancy to the ques tion of the powers of the Govern ing to transfer Begumbri land to an Taj Group. The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo when they decided to grant four acres Of Begumbli land which was not used for the main purpose of theZo for the construction of Five Star Hotels. It was also said that if, as the saying goes, the proof of the pudding is in the eating, the Chief Minister "s assurances are found reflected in the lease executed by the Taj Groups of Hotels in favour of the Govt. of WestBengal. The objection of the Public Undertakings Committee was first brought to the notice of the Minister for Metropolitan Development who submitted a note to the Chief Secretary pointing out that even if four acres were of land, out of the eight acres of Begambli land was given to the proposed hotels.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had two houses in Calcutta and the relevant date of valuation was 31st March 1957. The assessee had directed the company to debit his account to the extent of Rs.50,000. On 1.1.1957, the assessee made a gift of Rs 25,000 from his account. The gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's personal account in the books of account in respect of the firm whose accounts were said to be credited or debited. In the case of banking companies or other firms and companies who have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. The Income Tax Officer held that there was no valid gift of the principal amounts as there was a valid gift and therefore the assessee did not make any valid gift. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In reference, the High Court held that the gifts were valid and the interest paid in respect thereof could not be included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [130D] 2. In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in the accounts of the account in his books of accounts would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor. [131E F] 3. The fact that the assessee had made a valid gifts of Rs 50,000 to his son and to his wife respectively did not indicate that he was entitled to retain the possession and enjoyment of the property to tho entire exclusion of the donee or, to the entire exclusion from the exclusion of donor or, as the case may be. [132F G] 4. The entries in books of a bank by credit and debit, do not constitute valid gift but only make it clear that the transaction was genuine and there was nothing in them which could be said to have been credited in the account of the minor donees. [133G H] 5. In view of the fact that there is no registered deed and as there is a book entries in respect to the firm, the question whether there was valid gift or trust in respect thereto does not arise. [134A B] 6. The question whether the assessee has made a proper gift or a trust in favour of his son or relatives is a matter which must be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. [135C D] 7. In order to find out whether there is valid gift, the Court has to consider the effect of the entries in a particular book by credit or debit, and it is not necessary that the entries should be made contemporaneo nately or with such alterations as may be necessary for the purpose of ascertaining the real intention of the parties. [136E F; 137A] 8.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio Additional District and Sessions judges. In view of article 229 of the Constitution the power to appoint the secretaries to the Government is that of the Governor. Under the Government of India Act 1935, the power of transfer a district judge from one post to another was that of Governor though that power was always exercised in consultation with the High Court and by large on the recommendation of the High court. Obviously when the Governor promulgated the Orissa Superior judicial Service Rules 1963 he proceeded on the basis that the power could be transferred from one cadre to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work continue in that post for an unduly long time. The State Government implemented the orders in question on March 6 1967 and on October 10 1966, the Chief Secretary to the government of Orissa, the Home Secretary to Government of Orissa transferred all the officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district Judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other. The order of the State Government was set aside by the HighCourt in appeal. In these appeals by special leave it was contended that (1) the order of transfer passed by the State of Orissa is unsustainable because (a) the power under article 235 of the constitution is exclusively that of a Governor; (b) the Chief Justice is only concerned with the appointment, promotion and posting to the cadre which power is vested in the High Courts under article 233, though in consultation it with the high Court and (c) the control given to the High courts over district courts under that Article includes control over officers who preside over those courts. HELD: (1)(a) The High court must be held to have had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent or legal remonstrancer and member sales tax tribunal respectively on and after October 10, 1966 is set aside. [158 D] (b). The order transferring the District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power vested in it by article 235 as the control vested in that Article include control over the officers who presided over those Courts. [159 E F] (c).

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Gujarat on December 14, 1969. Its workmen were not entitled to sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of illness for which the employees claimed maternity leave. The workmen also felt aggrieved by the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Gujarat, dated September 24, 1975, in the dispute between them. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the ground that the benefit of sick leave was not available to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14. 1969 and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. The High Court held that the workmen are entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on full pay on the grounds of sickness. It also held that there was no practice of giving any such sick leave in the industries in Baroda or in the States of Gujarat, and that the appellant had not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that as the benefits granted by the Tribunal are not similar to those admissible under the Act, they are quite adequate and the Tribunal commit ted an error in granting them. HELD: (i) The scheme of the benefits admissible under section 49 of the , cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Industrial Tribunals. Section 61 of the Act does not provide for any leave to a workman on the basis of sickness, and even that amount is not admissible for the second time in the present case. [84 E] (ii) The Tribunal was justified in granting additional benefits to the workmen under the scheme. [85 G] (iii) The award in the instant case was made effective from December, 14,1969.
