[86 D E] Technological Institute of Textiles vs Its Workmen and others ; , followed.

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of his detention. He challenged the validity of the order based on the ground that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. It was not necessary for the detaining authorities to have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 22(5) and section 7 of the Act. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right Of representation and the obligation to supply particulars and the duty to considered whether the disclosed of any fact involved therein was against public interests. The requirement for such communication would depend on the facts of each case. In the present case there is no merit in this contention. (ii)The order of preventive detention was made without any real application of mind by the detaining Authority, that the authority acted only at the behest of the Police who were not in lete with the DeSte but also at the time of filing the affidavit. The fact that be bad made no such application for particulars is therefore a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration, in deciding whether the grounds can be considered to be invalid. (iii)The requirement for making a representation against his detention cannot be said to have been hampered by the non supply of particulars and failure to furnish the duty and to consider the sufficiency of such particulars would not vitiate the order.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was charged with having committed acts of gross misconduct. The Chief of the Army Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry, considered that the conduct of the appellant was most unbecoming of an officer. The Central Government directed removal from service of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal on the ground that r. 14 of the Defence Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the provisions of the Rules were ultra vires as they had been enacted by Parliament under Entry 41 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (ii) the words "subject to the Act" occurring in section 19 make section 19 subject to the provisions Of the Act and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from service any person subject to this Act. HELD : (1) The Army Rules, 1955, are ultra vires. They do not confer any power on the Central Govern ment to remove an officer without being tried by a court martial. [449 B] (2) The words " subject to" in section19 make section19 subject to section 45 and the Central government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions contained in section 45. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to this provision ' it speaks of removal of a person ' from the Service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. [448 C D] (3) The word "subject" used in section 20 makes section 19, subject to which the Central Govt. has no power. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under subject to other provisions of this Act, the central Government may remove a persons from the serv ice. Under section 19(2)(a) specifically gives power to make a rule providing for the removal from the ' service of persons subject to that Act. [450 C D]. (4) The expression "subject with the provisions" occurring therein in section 18 makes it clear that there should be rules and subject to such provisions as are applicable to the Central, Government may provide for.

The appellant was assessed to octroi duty under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court challenging the levy of octroi duty on the ground that it was not imported into the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale and that the appellant had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The High Court held that the tax was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed before the Standing Committee to fix octroi limits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 5 of the Taxes and Fees Rules framed under section 3(b) of the Act provides for appeals against levy or imposition of any tax or fee. The appellant has not shown that the Panchayat Samiti or the Standing committee had found sufficient facts to enable it to deal with the question. Therefore, the High court was right in holding that the levy was illegal and ultra vires. [222 B C] (ii) Rule 3(a) does not require the Panchayat to fix its octroi limits for consumption use or Sale. The expression "taxes on pilgrims" is used in a wide sense and includes all taxes levied and collected by a panchayat. The word "tax" has been defined in section 2(11) of C. P. & T. Act, 1947, as meaning the levy or collection of any duty or fee or tax. Therefore the fixing of the octroi limit with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy and the rules are not confined to octroi duties only. [223 E G] (iii) Rule 4(b), which authorises the levy is r. 22, does not contemplate that the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duty can start being levied. The fixing of octroi limits with the sanction of the Government is an important condition precedent for the levy. [225 B] (iv) Rule 6(b)(i) does require the Panchayats to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the Rules. The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in its order they have given very scanty facts and did not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [226 C D] (v) Rule 7(b). of the Rules requires that the notice following the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax, or fee, should be published by affixing a copy thereof in the office of the panchayat. If so read, it would mean that before the Octroi duty can commence being levied, r. 21 must be complied with.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government and that as 14 days had expired before March 18, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the meaning of section 12(6) of the Act. Held, that the provisions of sub section 2 Of section 20 of the , are applicable only when a report is received by an appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the reports under section 12 (6) are made by the Conciliation officer but when that report is receives by the Government, the appropriate government has to make its report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the State Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The provisions of section 20(2)(b) of Act 2 Of 1952 are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the Report of the Advisory Officer is received and the report is sent by the Inspector to the appropriate Govern ment. Colliery Labour Union Asanso vs Newerson Bissur Railway Co., , referredto. The Act does not affect the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal under section 20 (2)(a) of that Act.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he had been arrested in connection with a criminal case registered against him. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing by the petitioner and his associates, who were there to be killed. The detention order was served on or about 11th January, 1986. The petitioner challenged the order of detention before the High Court which dismissed the petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the order was passed on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups and that there were criminal cases against the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principles applicable in these types of preventive detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors., W.P.(Crl.) No. 3 96/86 with SLP (Crl) No. Crl A. 353/86 and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate Etah and others, ; , referred to. 2.1 The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. The principle applicable in those types of cases has been discussed and applied in the decision of Surajpal Sahu vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors. ; and Ramesh Singh vs District Magis trate Burdwan & Anr., ; , followed. 2:2 In the instant case, there were allegations of criminal cases which had been filed against the detenu. There was no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there Was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the detention order. If there were cogent materials for thinking that the detenu might have been released then these should have been made apparent. [910C D] 2.3 The grounds of detention were not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit of the District Magistrate, though there are indications that transfer of the detenu from one prison to another was considered but the need to serve the detention Order while he was in custody was not properly considered by the Detaining Authority in the light of the relevant factors. At least the records of the case do not indicate that. If that is the position, then however infirmityable the antecedents of a person might have be taken into considera tion by the detenu properly and effectively before the Service of the Order. [1010G H; 1011A] 2:4 In the present case, when the actual order of deten tion was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication in the petition that this fact or the questions that the alleged detenu might he released or was likely to be enlarged on bail. The service of detention order therefore, is not on valid consideration. [1110C] 2 :5 In the affidavit on behalf of the detaining author it has been stated that the petitioner was in Jail. There are allegations of mala fide against him and his activities were prejudicial to public order. In these circumstances, the continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. It is well settled in this constitutional framework that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a detenu for social defence.

The respondent assessee firm manufactures gold bars, i.e., manufacturers of shroffs and dealers in gold. The assessee firm manufactured gold bars and sold them to the dealers. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the respondent firm under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the ground that it suffered from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of Act, 1969 as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969, constitutionally invalid on the grounds that it suffers from the infirmity of excessive delega tion of legislative powers inasmuch as the restrictions which have been imposed in section 28 are meant to prevent circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object and reasons for exercising the power of discretion conferred on an Administrator by sec. 26(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. [955C] 1.2 In the instant case, the objective, the policy and the scheme of the enactment together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention Of the other provisions is clearly inapplicable. The object, therefore, is not to provide any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. Even the restriction imposed by sec 28 is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry on the business in licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the act in making his orders. [936F G] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; , followed. 1.3 The object of the Urban Ceiling Act is to provide for the acquisition of goods lending, Banking or any kind of foreign business, for the control of production, manufacture, supply distribution, use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. [951B] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthia & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. 1:4 The object is not the same as the administrator can have to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec. 24(6).

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli District. The said lands were alienated from time to time and as a result of the last alienation, the appellants became entitled to them. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants claiming a declaration that they had acquired title by adverse possession. The trial Court found that the grant was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951. On appeal, the lower appellate court held that the lands were granted in Inam to the respondents and they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The High Court also held that it could not be said that the appellants had acquired a title by hostile possession prior to 1st January 1929. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the facts proved in the present case did not show that the alienees had been removed from management of the temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. It is open to doubt whether the said decision could lead to the inference that if a part of the property was transferred by the manager on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowments, the transfer is void ab initio, with the result that the possession of the transferee is adverse to the temple from the very beginning. [693 D E] (ii) The fact that the alienation made by the appellants in favour the respondents was for a valuable consideration does not affect the application of article 134 B of the Limitation Act. It only applies to cases where it is shown that the immovable property was comprised in the endowment and that the transfer was for valuable consideration. [651 C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the title of the respondents had not been lost by adverse posses sion before the suit was filed. [641 D] (iv) The contention that the transfers with which we are concerned in the instant case fall outside the purview of article 135 B is without substance. It does not mean that the intention of the legislature must be gathered from the language used and the words used therein must be understood in their ordinary sense. In construing a statute, it is necessary to bear in mind the object of the Act. The words used are "transfer effected by a previous manager on behalf of the public". If the property is transferred by a manager not as manager but as an individual, he has no longer any interest in the property and his right to challenge the transfer would be lost if his predecessor who made the transfer lives for more than 12 years after effecting the transfer.

The appellant, who was the owner of a cinema theatre in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the District Magistrate and the appellate authority under the Jammu & Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, so long as there had not been any transfer of the license by the original licensees to another with the sanction of the licensing authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though the licence had been granted in favour of Ved Gupta and not in favour M/s. Krishan Kumar, the license was still subsisting and that the license having been granted by the competent authority in favour the appellant, he did not have the possession of the premises and therefore could not claim a renewal of his licence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by District Magistrate directing the suspension of the cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. They had no legal right whatever to conduct the cinema show in the theatre without a licence in contravention of the law. [582B] 2.1 The High court was wrong in holding that since the license granted by M/S. Ved Gupta was in favour a partnership consisting of himself and his partners, it necessarily follows that where the licensed premises including the cinematograph used therein belonged to a partnership and one of the partners obtains a licence, in his individual capacity, he alone is the licensee. [591C D] 2:2 The license granted in respect of the Apsara Theatre was in the nature of a licence for the premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the appellant Nagar Nagar, Jammu and Nagar, and that it necessarily followed that where a licensed premises includes the partnership, the other partners automatically acquire interest in the licence and that in the absence of any legal right or legitimate expectation being available to the petitioners, there was no obligation on the part of the District Magis trate to afford them a hearing before passing the impugned order. [592F G] 2(a) The High Courts have consistently taken the view that where an application for a licence is made by a partnership firm and one or more partners obtains licences in his separate name, the others automatically acquire interests in the licensee and that such rights are granted to them in his personal and individual capacity. [593B C] (b) In the instant case, the licence was granted by District Magi trate in favour Apsar Mal, the appellant. The licence was a valid one and the license could not have been cancelled on the ground of its being the sole licensee. The impugned order was therefore violative of principles of natural justice. [595C D; 594D] (c) The impugned orders were passed by a District Magistrate in exercise of his function of administering the provisions of the Act and the Rules and the implied power to take all steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute. [596F G]. (d) The order was not one suspending the licence issued in respect thereof. It was only the licensee who had no authority in law to conduct such exhibition of films. There was no suspension of a license issued in favour B, and the impugned orders passed against him were therefore illegal.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to them under section 12 of the , stating that they had systematically committed breaches of various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them. The appellants challenged the validity of the notice, contending that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 10 of the Act and that the notice was ultra rites. Held, that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 13 of the . The provisions of the section clearly indicate that the Custodian has the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. But he con tended that the powers conferred on him by section 12 could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease was held, and this result flows according to him from the language of the non obstante clause which is limited to anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, , applied. The operative portion of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be made "notwithstanding anything containedin any other Law for the lime being in existence". The operative part of the Section which confers powers on the custodian to cancel contracts created not only by the evacuee and not by himself, but also on him.

The respondent was a minor son of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for the appellant in respect of his father and allotted him to the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate Authority which allowed the same on the ground that the appellant was in possession of 112 Bighas only and not 129 Bighas and 3 Biswas as held by the lower courts. In a revision application preferred by the respondent, the Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on the grounds that the petitioner was in posses sion of 112 bighas only and that he was in pos session of 112. Bighas even though he was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divi sional Officer on 5th May, 1976. The Board went on to hold that there is no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1973. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, the respondent contended that no appeal having been filed by him against the order, the said order became final and the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the sub Divisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 221 of the Indian Tenancy Act provides for executive powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. It is open to the Board to exercise its powers of supervision on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of 'the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open for the Board or Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. A similar question arose before this Court in Kana and others vs Board of revenue, Rajasthan, ILR [1973] 1 S.C.R. 884 (F.B.) and Kana and Others vs Board Of Revenue, Rajasthan; ILR [1974] 1 All. E.R., 981 (F). In the instant case, the appellant had been in possession on 14th March, 1963 and was only thirteen years of old age when he was admittedly minor son. The order passed by the Board was set aside by the High Courts. [726C D] 2.1 There is no restriction on the powers of the Board under section 221 of Indian Evidence Act to set at naught the judicial orders of the courts. [ 728D E] 2:2 There is nothing illegal in law in the order dated 14th April, 1975 passed by a subordinate court. The appellant had not filed an application for adducing additional evidence in support of his contention.

The first respondent, a journalist, was engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports. The first respondent filed an application before the Central Government under section 12 of the , praying for the benefits conferred upon him by the Act. The Central Government rejected the claim of the first respondent and held that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law reports published were not newspaper as defined in the Act, and that they were not the newspapers within section 2 (b) and therefore the orders made by them were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two courts reports published in the law report were not presses but only newspaper reports which could be said to contain news so as to become newspaper. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first Respondent in their production or publishing of the law Reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Govern ment on the based on the recommendations made by Paleakar Award. [778C] 2. The expression "newspaper" is not defined in section 2 of the . The law report which are to be published by a newspaper and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Though the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper, the publication does not cease to be a newspaper within the definition of "new 'paper ' in the . [780E F] 3. The word "new" is used in the sense of "an journalist". It is not understood in the context of any particular case whether newspaper or newspaper is a newspaper. The term "newly closed" has been defined by section 2 to mean any person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. [783G] 4. The definition of the expression "Newspaper ' is usually applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current events and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, and journals which in so faras they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets and both into one another. [784C D] 5. The publication of items by themselves may not be a substantial portion of a newspaper report to making it a paper, but the publication is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper which may after some time cease to he a newspaper or become a book of reference.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th February, 1966 a fresh document was executed and it was alleged that the appellant continued by virtue of that agreement. The appellant filed an application for eviction against the respondent on the ground that he was a sub tenant of a business concern. The trial Judge passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st March, 1988. The High Court refused to interfere with the finding of the trial court that the respondent was a licensee and not a subtenant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the appellant was not a tenant as such or licensee; (2) the Court of Small Causes Bombay had no jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case; and (3) the court of Small Cause Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of High Court that the Respondent was a tenant is a licence and not licence. good deal of submission was made before this Court that if it was a lease and not license then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the court had to jurisdiction and there was no estoppel. [21D] 2. The expression "B.C."" was used in section 15A on the 1st day of February, 1973. The word "B C" is used in the context of the Act. In order to get the advantage of section 15 A of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the premises as a licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the Ist of February 1973. But if he was not merely a licensee under a subsisting agreement on the first day of January, 1973 then he did not get the benefit of the amended provision of the said Act. [22E F] 3. The Court of Appeal in England again in Cobb vs Lane, ; , held that where it cannot be said that there was a clear error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [23F G] 4. In view of the fact that the parties had been carrying on business for some time, it was not possible to determine whether the appellant proved himself to be a sub lessee or not. The question whether the respondent is a tenant or licensee depends upon the construction of the document and the facts and circumstances of this case. [24F G; 25A] 5. In the instant case, the appellant had been in occupation for some period prior to the termination of his tenancy. It was a licence which he could have obtained under the Rent Act. The respondent had not proved that he had gone to occupy the suit property any time before that date and the dispute started only from the date of the agreement. In fact, the rent light bill stood in the name of the respondent showing that there were no desire to create any lease by the document mentioned therein and the appellant regarded him as a mere licensee. The tenancy was not for a sub lease. [25G H; 26A] 6. The background of the facts of this ease is clear from the entire document negate the contention of the appel lant that it was merely a licence. The document created an interest in the property, it is a license and not as a lease. good dealing of submission made before the trial Court was a license. [26B] 7.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute between him and the State of Rajasthan related to a time before merger of former Dhol Purshat in 1949. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned, were taken away from the former princely State into the United State of Rajaswa and thereafter the former State of Dholpur came to be included in the United States of Rajasthan through the Matsya Union. The respondent claimed that he had been granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni from the latter State on the basis of an agreement dated January 26, 1950, which was entered into by him with the Government of India and which was accepted by the Government. The suits were resisted by the State on various grounds but the High Court held that the liability of the State to refund the amount collected in advance for no export was not fasten on the respondent as it emerged from the agreement dated February 26,1950, and therefore the State was bound by the obligation of the latter to refund it. The State appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the liability to refund could only be determined by the Ruler of the erstwhile prince State of Jaipur, and (2) the agreement had been recognised by the new sovereign and therefore article VI of the Covenant could not operate to confer any right on the company as against the new State. HELD : (i) The new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 onwards was in its entirety an act of State and that article VI did not apply to it. [179 E] (ii) The agreement dated 26th January 1950, was a mere recognition of the rights of the subjects and the new Government had no right to recognise them as sovereigns and that the new state assumed liabilities of the old laws and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part B State of Jodhpur. [180 G] (iii) The appellant could not be allowed to raise a contention in this Court that the agreement was recognised by it. It is true that in the present case the new Ruler had been recognition by the New State throughout this period and under section 3 of the covenant, all the assets and liabilities of tho Covenanting States were to be the assets of the new States must have intended to respect all the rights flowing from laws so continued and assume all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. [181 G] Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The State of Saurashtra, ; , followed.

The appellants were dealers in commercial crops. They sold their produce to a third party at the market rate and paid the price of the commodity to them. The appellants contended that they were not entitled to any deduction under section 14 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, as amended by the Amending Act of 1955, because, they had only two fundamental rights: (1) that they did not achieve the object for which they were enacted but were also prohibited from holding their business as property; and (2) that the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder constituted reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to do business. Held, that the appellants were not liable to pay any tax under the Madras Sales Tax Act, 1939, as it was not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 Of the Act. The provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the impugned Act read with the bye laws framed thereunder showed that the Act did not impose reasonable restrictions upon the appellants ' fundamental right to carry on business and therefore they were valid. The Act did provide for the better regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops in the Presidency of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The object of the provisions was to eliminate, as far as possible, the middlemen and to give reasonable facilities for the growers of commercial crop to secure best prices for their commodities. The fact that the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the provi sions under section 15 of the , did not make any difference in the matter. The impugned provisions of Act, as they stood before the amendment of 1955 by the amending Act of 1956, showed that there was no restriction on a person 's rights to do trade or business and that the restrictions imposed were reasonable. The imposition of the tax was therefore valid.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions and sentences. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) the conviction should be maintained but the sentence in each case should be reduced to transportation for life; (2) the appellants were not guilty and so should be acquitted of the offence under section 34 of the Penal Code; and (3) the High Court erred in holding that the death sentences on the three appellants were illegal. HELD : The conviction must be maintained. The sentence of imprisonment for a term of ten years will suffice. That leaves the question of sentence in the case of Bhilia and Tukia. It is not enough as in the present case, to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, or, as the case may be, to determine the conclusion on the facts in another. All that is necessary is either to have a direct proof or proof, of circumstances, which necessarily leads to that conclusion, or ,, as it prefer to put it in the time honoured way, "the incriminating facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis". The case of the appellants was not one of mere preponderance of accusation but one of a strong character. [1091 H; 1092 A B] In the present ease, the circumstances disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in the instant case. There is no evidence to show that there were any prior meeting. It was also not proved that the appellants had been guilty and convicted of the murder. The conviction of the appellant must be set aside.

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer under the Ministry of Works and Housing in the Central Public Works Department on 22.10.1947. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 made under Rule 56(j) of Fundamental Rules. The vires of Rule 56 (j) was challenged before this Court by the petitioner who was a Section officer in the Ministry. This Court held that the impugned order was contrary to the judgment delivered by this Court and did not require to be re examined. It was further held that Rule 56 was meant to cover only those who were in a post on a regular basis i.e. in a regular manner, i. e., in a class or Class II service or post. The petitioner had crossed the age of 50 years but had not attained the age Of 55 years by the date of the order. This court held that it was meant for the benefit of all Government servants and sub clause (i) carves out a class of Government servants into a category and makes a special provision. It further held in Tahiliani 's case that sub clause(ii) did not apply to the facts of this case as the petitioner had not attain the age at the time of retirement. The Court also observed that sub cl.(i) was not attracted to the case because the petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class I or Class 11 service or a post, on substantive basis. On this conclusion the writ petition was allowed and the order of compulsory retirement made against each of the petitioners was set aside. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The ratio of the decision in Tahilani ' 's Case is not correct and sub cl (i). of Rule56(j)(1) applies to Government servants in Class l or Class I service or posts on substantive, temporary or offi cial basis. [637C] 2. Sub clause (ii) of Rule 55(j), which applies to government servants in class I or class II service and post on substantive. temporary oroffi ciating basis, is meant to covers only those Government servants who are in Class 1 or Class III service or Post, on officiating basis. Instances are abundant where officers are promoted to Class I and Class II Service or posts in such a service or office as covered by sub clause 2. The possibility of such incumbent being sent back to the substantive post is not at all relevant in the matter of exercising powers of compulsory retire ment.

The respondents, who were the husband of respondent No. 1 and father of respondent Nos. 2 to 5, filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on the ground that the medical examination report was not submitted by the doctor in charge of the deceased and that the deceased had fulfilled his part of the insurance contract and the appellant corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards premium payable by the deceased. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondents were entitled to claim the amount along with interest at six per cent per annum from the date of refusal of payment till the date on which the demand was made and that it was not necessary for them to have any cause of action. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was a concluded contract between the deceased 's husband and the Corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the appellant. On the other hand, there was an express provision in the Financial Powers Act, 1960 dealing with the financial powers. Indeed there was nothing in the Act which would justify a conclusion of the High court that there is a concluded agreement. The expression "underwrite" signifies acceptance by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [359E F] In the instant case, the appellant had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager, to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. The Trial Court was therefore right in holding the appellant guilty of the charge and that he should have been acquitted. [360F G] 2.1 In view of the fact that such a long time has elapsed and further in view of finding that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal, the plea of Divisional manager being a mere formality is accepted. Acceptance must be signified by some acts or acts con cerned on by parties or through their agents from which it is possible and communicates his acceptance to the person making the offer. Whether the final acceptance is that of the assured or insurers, however, depends simply on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have progressed.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V. L. R. 60 IA. 76. The trial court granted an interim order restraining encashment of the letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. In appeal, the High Court set aside the order and remanded the case to the trial court for trial. On remand, the trial Court passed a decree in favour and directed the appellant to take steps in execution of the decree. The High Court held that an order granting interim injunction was a final order as far as this Court is concerned and that it was not necessary for the High Courts to give any direction to grant interim injunction. In the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) An order passed by the High court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). The expression "final order" in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an interlocutory order passed in a proceeding. [701 B C] (2) An interim injunction cannot be granted unless it is final. In a suit pending before the High 'Court, an order deciding that circumstances had not been established such as would justify an order for stay of execution of a decree under appeal was not a final decision on the rights of the party in dispute in the suits or proceeding. If after the order is made, the suit is still left alive and has got to be tried, and the rights in disputes have to be determined, the order being interlocutory. [700 C D] (3) The expression 'final order ' in section 206 of the Code of Civil Procedure means a final adjudication on the merits of the dispute in a suit. An order under section 205 is an interlocutory one and is final within its meaning. [601 G H] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, ; , followed. (4) The order refusing to grant an interim relief did not determine the rights or obligations of parties in relation to the matter in dispute. [071 C D]. Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, A.I.R. 1958 S.C. 1017, referred to.

The appellant company was manufacturing processed fabric and manufac turing the processed fabric. The excise authorities treated the value of the processed fabrics as the assessable value of processed fabric, and assessed the same to duty under section 3(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. The Assistant Collector confirmed the demand of duty on the basis that the value was the assessablevalue of the grey cloth in the hands of the processor plus the value thereof. On appeal by the appellant company, the Tribunal held that the assessable valuation of the goods should be the value for the purpose of the excise duty and not the value which would be taken to be the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market. Dismissing the appeal by Revenue, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessable value is the value as determined by the Assistant Collector of Central Excise under section 4(1). [346C] 2. The valuation of goods owned by one person are manufactured by another and the information is required relating to the price of the processing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [346D] 3. The factory gate as if the processed cloth was sold by the processor. In order to explain the position it is made clear that the market value of goods should not be the valuation under the Act and the rules made thereunder. [347E] 4. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the fabric as to what would be the prices at which they would be sold in the open market, that would be taking by the Excise authorities as the valuation of such goods and not any further subsequent profit. It was not necessary to add the trader 's profit to the concept of the price for the grey fabrics or fabric plus the values of the job work done plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On March 14, 1975 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975, he was again promoted as Head Clerk. The Punjab Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Government. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appel lant to the post of a Head clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be promoted as an Assistant or a Head Clerks. He is appointed lawfully to the posts of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [738C D] 2. The appellant was promoted on ad hoc appointment prior to June 13. 1975, but he was not confirmed in the Government service. Since the appellant had been appointed without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post. [750D E] 3. Even if it is assumed for the purpose of argument, that the rights to be consti tuted are a term, and condition is of service what is applicable for our purposes is not that the appell lant was entitled as he was appointed lawfully. He had been promoted as Assistant or Head Clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, he became entitled to continued in the serv ice of the Government on the date on which it purported to do so.

The appellant was the Mahant of a Math, and installed a deity acclaimed by the name of "Gokarneshwar Mahadeo" installed in the Math. The property was purchased by the Mahant from his predecessor Shivshankar Yati. The income tax authorities assessed the appellant to income tax for the years 1951 52 and 1952 53 on the basis that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that the appellant was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The High Court allowed the appeal of the appellant holding that the Amauli properties had been purchased by Shivshanker Yati from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessors in interest and that he was entitled to possess, enjoy and acquire personal property. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclean Yati; that the income tax from the properties belonging to the math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan, deepdan, daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaulty properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivsarayan Yati and did not form part of the properties of the Math, Sauna. [663G] 2. In assessment proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amauri properties constitute the personal properties of Mahant Shiva Shankar Yati, and do not form parts of the property of the math Sauna nor of the deity. Small parcels of these properties were transferred by Mahant Shiv Shedutha to the appellant 's predecessor in interest. The properties were purchased by him for Rs. 40,000 from his successor Shivswar Ji Maharaj. He was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Varanasi, in respect of the two fixed deposits made by him in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shiv shankar Yat, who executed a will in 1956 bequeathing certain properties to the deity with the intent that arrangements for bhog would be met from them. The appellant was granted succession certificate under section 6 of the U P. Agricultural Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1964. Mahant Shiva Shanker Yati died on November 12, 1924 and his heirs were brought on record as legal representatives. The question whether the fund was the personal or separate funds left behind by his predecessor ininterest was not raised before the High Court. [665B C] 3. The appeal is dismissed.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. The Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab cancelled the allotment of certain quasi permanent allottees of evacuee property in the same district on the ground that they had been wrongly fitted in the village released upon cancellation of allotment of land in their favour by reason of cancellation of the allotment in their names. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General but the same was rejected on the grounds that r. 102 of the Rules framed under section 12(1) of the Act empowered the Central Government to acquire evacuee property for rehabilitation of displaced persons by publishing in the official gazette a notification to that effect, and that the notification issued thereunder was invalid as it had been made after the commencement of the , and the notification was therefore invalid. The High Court dismissed the revision application on the view that r, 102 did not apply to the case because the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land at all. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (i) the Custodian had no power under section 10(1), to cancel the allotment; (ii) the notification dated March 24, 1955 issued by the Central Govern ment under section 13(1)(a) of Act 1 of 1954 was invalid because the order of cancellation was erroneous and (iii) the cancellation of allotments was a colourable exercise of powers. HELD : (1) The Custodian had not been in possession at the critical time they would have had the right to obtain a permanent transfer in their name. [337 B] (a) The provisions of section 19(1 ) of the Punjab Act do not apply because the power of the Custodian under section 19 is confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. Therefore, even if no managing officer or managing corporation was appointed with respect of that property no one else could exercise the power. [333 C] (b) The fact that subsequent to the issue of the notification under section 11(1). of the .the Act, the property would cease to be evacuee property and the said powers of the custodian would be in conflict with those conferred by section 19 of the 1954 Act on a managing officer and managing corporation. [332 G] (c) The contention that there was no entrustment in fact of this property or this class of properties to a managing agent or managing Corporation could not be accepted.

The State Public Service Commission issued a notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Care ments) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Dulaji ousalodian of Girls schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (earch) District Inspecto rised by the State Government on May 5, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985, which was published in the newspapers and was published again on June 9, 1985 and was also published on the same day. The selection process was completed in two stage written and interviews/personals test. The appellant State Public Services Commission rejected the claim of the appellants for re holding the recruitment examination. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. [125B C] 1.2 The State Public Serv ices Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not be suffered. Public interest has been appropriately considered by setting down the four year in the instant case. [126C D] 2.1 The State Government should have be more careful to set aside the selection and asking the High Court for a re holding of it. [127D E] 2:2 In the instant cases, when no defect had been pointed out, the High Courts could have directed that the order of the Public Service Com mission cancelling the entire recruitment examination be quashed. The State Commission should also have been less careful in deal ing with the matters so that 4 years in tact would not hav er affected the selection. On account of improper feeding into the computa tion some of the candidates who had better performance in the viva voce were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the examination were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Services Com mission should have acted in a more careful manner by setting it aside. [ 127E F] 2 :3 The State of Uttar Pradesh has been properly met by set aside candidates who have better performance.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga and the other at Nanga Kheri. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed it holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The High Court further held that after taking evidence, the appellant could not be said to have any knowledge about the date of death of the widow. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The suit against the person upon whom the interest had devolved was sought to be continued against Shiam Das as de facto mahant of the Dera after the demise of Som Das. [488B] 1.2 In the instant case, the suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties attached to it. The appellant had no right to recover possession of the property of theDera. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [489C D] 1:3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest in property i,e.,, the subject mater of the Suit and the interests is the interests of the person who was the party to the suit. It was, however, contended on behalf of the respondent that there is no devolution of interest in tho subject matter in the suit on death of a previous mahant by virtue of law or custom that there would be devolution of inter est in the subject of the claim of the appellant. When the suit is filed by oragainst a person, in a represen tative capacity and the appeal is sought to he continued against the persons acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court, it cannot be continued under Order 22 rule 10, because the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. [490C E] 2.1 In the present case, there was no certainty as to the person whom would become the mahant if he was elected to be the Mahant of the dera after his death. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiamdas was elected as mahant. The appeal could not therefore be continued by the respondent.

The Andhra Pradesh State and Karnataka had framed the Andhra Pradesh Civil Service (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1979. The validity of these rules was challenged by some of the petitioners who were working as Junior Engineers in the Andhra State. They contended that the age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years with effect from October 29, 1979 after an elaborate and scientific inquiry by a committee constituted under Rule 2 of the Andhra Civil Service Rules, and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age. The Government of Andhra Pradesh rejected their claim for premature retirement on the ground that they were not competent to reduce their age. It was contended that there was no basis at all for reducing the age as it was arbitrary and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the Governor under Article 309 is a legislative power and the Legislature has the power to make provision for removing the difficulty arising in the exercise of such power. [655E] 1.2 The Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the retirement age at 58. It is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. The recommendation of the Second Central Pay Commission that the retirement should be raised from 55 and that the said recommendation was accepted by the State Government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect form the date of retirement. [557F G] 1:3. The fact that the decision to reduce the age is taken by the Government cannot justify the conclusion that it is arbitrary because it is unscientific in the sense that it was not backed by due investigation or by compilation of relevant data on the subject. If reduction of retirement age from 58 to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the grounds that it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [60G H] 1 :4. The question whether the exercise by the Governor of Andhra pradesh was arbitrary or irrational and unconnected to the object of the Act has to be kept out of consideration in so far as the question of the power of compulsory retirement is concerned. [61C D] 2.1 It is well settled that the power conferred on the Governor by Article 309 can be exercised only for good reasons and not for any other purpose. The power to retire a Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to Last Grade Service, shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the are of 55 years. [62E F] 2:2 It is difficult to appreciate how the exercise undertaken by the High Court of power can be challenged as lacking in authority. The recommendations made by the Second Pay Commission were not accepted by Government initially because it felt that raising the age at 55 was a fair and reasonable basis. The report of the Commission has therefore to be treated as a valid exercise of legislative power.

The appellants are dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana. They purchased raw materials inside the State and exported those goods out of India. The respondent assessee purchased raw material inside the state from outside the State but paid no tax thereon, as they were registered dealers and furnished the declaration forms prescribed under section 24(1)(b) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessing authority assessed the appellant to sales tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of that Act. This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that: (i) the words "in the course of export outside India" in section 5(1), are used in the context of sales falling under sub section (3) but not under sub s.(1) thereof, and (ii) the expression "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later on, clause (b) is used in relation to a sale or purchase within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "for the purpose of export" in sub s(1). are used with reference to sales and purchases that form part of his taxable turnover. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 5 but the goods presently in question are not exigible to tax. [353B] 2. The expression "for sale" is defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in the course oY of inter state trade or commerce". [353D] 3. The word "export" has been used in section 4(1 ) and not in sub section 2 (c). The expression 'sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act ' means the taking out from the state to any places outside it, otherwise than in the way prescribed by section 5. [354E] 4. The language of section 9 (1) (a) and (b), as amended, is clear and unambiguous. It uses the words 'within the meaning ' in sub sec tion (1). The words 'in the case of goods which are not specified in Schedule B ' mean "the take out of tho goods specified in schedule B" but not in the form of a sale in that category. [355F] 5. The definition of "turnover" in Section 2(p) of section 2 is inclusive and includes within it, the taking Out of the taxable turnover under section 15, is only imposed on the sales and purchase price of any goods on the sale of which tax is levied under this act though the assessees are exempt from payment of such tax by reason of section 24 (1), [355G] 6. The Explanation to sub sec.(1). provides that a dealer registered under this section shall also be entitled to purchase, without payment of sales tax, at the rate notified under section 3, "the purchase value" of any 'goods on the Sales Tax Appeal No. 894/76 dated 31.3.1983 and the purchase price in the case the goods are specified in the Schedule B. The proviso thereto provides that where a dealer who purchases goods without payment or otherwise than under sub sec. (1)(a) of s 5, he shall be liable to pay tax on such sale at the rates notified under Section 15(3). [355H; 355A] 7. The explanation to section 9 of the Punjab General Sales tax Act, 1948 provides that "the sale proceeds of any good leviable under the Act" shall not include the purchase goods, that form parts of his gross turnover are included in Schedule A and that he is liable to be taxed on the purchases effected by him but for a claim for exemption under section 25.

The appellant firm was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The goods were sent to the sellers by the sellers on board the ship and they were delivered to the buyers on board. The sellers returned the goods to the seller on the ground that these sales were not their property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim for exemption and assessed them to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the grounds that they remained the sellers ' property till they were brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). The appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In further appeals to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the goods remained the seller 's property till after they had crossed customs barrier, and that therefore the exemption under article286(1) will come into operation. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words " the time of the export" mean the time when the goods cross the customs frontier. The word " a registered dealers" is wide enough and includes a registered firm. In the United Motors case, the goods were on shipped by the seller and the contract was that payment will be made on the presentation of the bill of lading. The contract being that payment would be made at the time the goods reached the destination, the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sold to a registered person. The fact remains that the intention declared has not been carried out. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Act no purchase tax was leviable from them under article 285(1).

The respondent wife married the appellant 's second wife. She was a second wife and had a son by her. The first wife died in 1956. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. The respondent filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 against the appellant and his father. The Magistrate found that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ . The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that the woman has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there should be proof for maintenance. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 'S.127 rescue the respondent from his obligation. Payment of mehar money as a customary discharge is within the cognisance of that provision. But what was the amount of mehari ? Rs. 5000/ , interest from which could not keep the woman 's body and soul together for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul. The husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 127(3) of Cr. P.C. [79 C D] 2. The expression "in which a marriage otherwise eligible, is entitled" in section 125 means a woman who has been divorcee by or had obtained a decree from her court and has neither claimed nor remarried". It does not mean that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence based on mehar payment, merits more serious attention. [80 E F] 3. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code. [81 G H] 4. If one were to locate a legal ground to raise the contention that the wife was not living separately by mutual consent, the court has spoken nothing to the contrary; and The High court has not spoken at all. Moreover, the husband has failed to prove his right to ignore the payment of the sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [82 C D].

The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 under which he was directed to black list the appellant. The said order was challenged by the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the black listing of the appellant was not specifically mentioned in the order and that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the State that there is no requirement specifically of giving any notice under the rule of giving an opportunity to the appellant as he had been given a show cause notice and that the cancellation of the bid of the appel lant was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing order passed by the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not affected. This order will, however, not prevent the State Govt. or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for cancelling the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law. [868C D] 1.2 The order of the Collector dated 25th 3 1988 is set out in verbatim below: "Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Thakur, Village Repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur has bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Singh S/O Late Gorakh Nath Village Repudwara, Pages. 1.3 The cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned. That is not effected. [886D E] 2. The order dated 25.3 1988 of the Collec tor is set quashed. So long as the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing the appellant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law.

The appellant was the tenant of certain co owners. The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises leased to him under two lease deeds dated 22 9 1947 and 3 10 1947. The first lease deed provided that the lessee was entitled to seek fixation of the fair rent at Rs. 150 per month. The second lease deed also provided that if the lessee did not pay the rent for three months, he would be liable to eviction from the leased premises. The Rent Controller held that the buildings on the land leased under two leases were conveyed to the appellant and that the appellant was entitled only to seek fix of fair rents in respect thereof. On appeal, the appellate authority confirmed the order of the Rent Controller. In further revision, the High Court held that since the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation or fixation of rent in view of the provisions of section 64 C of the Act and that therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Act was not maintainable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that since he was only an intermediary, the rent could not be determined without jurisdiction, although it would have to be decided by the Rent Tribunal as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the denial of the landlord 's title by the tenant is bona fide or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [562D] 1.2 In order to decide whether the refusal of a landlord ' s title by a tenant is bonafide, the Court has to consider the nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Controller under the Act. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner of property seeks to evict his tenant under section 10(2)(vii) but the Rent controller refuses to pass the order for eviction though satisfied about his title because the tenant had acted bona fide, it would be open to the owner to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [561E F] 1:3. The jurisdiction of the Controller, under section 11(4) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Conversion) Act 1948, is a statutory jurisdiction which is vested in the Rent control ler by the terms of the . It will not be open for the High Courts to entertain a collateral attack on the validity of binding nature or correctness of the order passed by the Court of Small Causes and to consider and determine afresh the issue as to whether the tenant has title adjudicated on the question. [560F G] 1 :4. The decision of the Additional Settlement Officer that the suit land was sold to the appellants and that they were entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, is not final on the issue that opens up his jurisdiction and cannot preclude an owner from contending in a Civil Court, that he should not be asked to pay rent for his own property to some one else. [559G H] 1 5. The question of title to the property is one on which his very jurisdiction depends. In order that a tenant may have to establish his contention on the basis of the evidence adduced by him, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the landlords on the strength of the same evidence. It would not be right to contend that the order in the earlier proceedings is to be treated as an order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and effect of the decision in the first set of proceedings. [558C D] 1 6.

The Mysore State Civil Service Integra tion Rules, 1960 provide for filing objections to the preliminary list. The petitioner was given ample opportunity to object to the final list. He filed objections to a final list on an analogy with the second opportunity which was granted to him. The High Court held that the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, was ultra vires and illegal and directed the re spondents to get opportuni ty of puting forward their objections before final list was prepared. [828 C] (iii)The High Court was right in holding that the conclu sioner had ample opportunities to make a representation with regards the two points urged by him and the Supreme Court had also to give a full and fair opportuni ties to the parties affected to make their representations; and the Central Govern ment has also to furnish a full, and fair opportunity to the respondents affected to makes their representations.
