The petitioners, a partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds, filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution in this Court challenging the validity of sub para (10) of Para 218 of the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 and also for a direction to the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import Policy 197879. The petitioners contended that sub para(10) was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which were prohibited for import by the holder of an Additional Licence, and that the word "banned" was intended only to take into account those items which are excluded under the Export Policy, 1978 79 but also from importing items excluded under Appendices 3 and 5 Part A of the said Policy. The respondents contended that the petitioners had failed to achieve the objective of granting the Additional Licences and the import policy and that there was no similarity between them and other persons who were granted Additional licences on the basis of their exports made during the period 1977 78 in accordance with the Import and Export Policy 1988 91, and the Export Houses who would be granted Additional Licences on or after April 1, 1988, on the ground that they had failed in the export of "other products" during the year 1977 78. The writ petitions were contested by the respondents contending that sub Para (10), para 218 of para 218 was intended for taking in terms of Import & Exports Policy 1978 80 and that under the said policy the basis for grant of Additional Licences was the f.o.b. value of exports, and not the Export House which was to be given on the strength of the order dated April 18, 1985. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners who were holders of Additional licences under the Imports & Exports Control Policy 1978 1979 79 have been granted an Additional Licences whereunder it is permissible to import items as per para 215 of the Export and Import Policy 1985 91 on the view that the petitioner 's claim for additional licence cannot be said to be persons similarly circumstanced. Under the Import Trade Policy 1978, there were two requirements for grant or renewal of Additional Licence: one was the condition that the value of the imports made by the Import House for the purpose of exporting goods is to be excluded from the fringed benefits of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendice (in Appendicating) Order 1978 79.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at the material time in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, and there fore, the goods were sold in bulk and delivered to customers at the appellant 's factory. The appellant had filed price lists in respect of the same. In respect of such consignments, the appellant was required to pay duty on the value of the drums manufactured by it. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that the goods are not returnable and hence the value could not be included in the assessable value. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the good were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the packing was not returnable to the buyer; there fore the value had to be included as per the definition of "value" in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the order of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing contemplated in section 9(4) (d)(ii) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 for determining the "value", in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such packings" and not value. Therefore, it was held that where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of excisable goods, while determining the value, the cost of such packing would be includible in the value for assessment to excise duty. However, if any special secondary packing is provided by the assessee at the in stance of a wholesale buyer which is not generally provided as a normal feature of the wholesale trade, the costs of such special packing would not be includible. [995E F] 1.2 The cost incurred by the manufacturer and recovered by him from the purchaser whether as part of the sale price or separately, cannot be included under section 4 (4)(a) of Act. [996F G] 1:3. In construing section 4 of the Central Excises and Salt Act it is necessary to bear in mind that the measure of excise duty is price and not the value. The nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods arc sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessablevalue, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant was charged with having committed food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued his practice before the notice was issued to him. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in a canteen for three days and he was demanding bribe of Rs. 100. On 21.10,1975, the appellant was alleged to have pressed the demand to PW 1. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and section 336 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appel lant was guilty. It is not a case that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant in his possession as a money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [357B] 2. The evidence of PW 1 is clearly incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW l. This Court observed that though the conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5 (1)(a) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I.p.c. The accused had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [340D] Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1, referred to.

The respondent company was a public limited company. It had been running its flat for six months after the expiry of its employment and had been required to pay compensation for use of the premises. The company was compelled to leave the premises in the company 's flat for 6 months after its retirement and in accordance with the company "s rules, he was required to make a declaration that he was wrongfully withholding the property of the company. In view of this, the company was constrained to lodge a complaint against the petitioner under section 630 of the Act in the Court of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 37th Court Esplanade Bombay alleging that he had wrongfully withheld the flat in question which had been given to him for his residence during the period of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 6(1) (a) of the . The company 'was constrained to file a complaint before the Additional chief Metropolitan Magistrate. The Company Judge held that it was not necessary to make any declaration as contemplated by section 630(l)(b) of H.P. Act, 1947 and accordingly issued process under sub section (2) of section 630. The High Court also took the view that the words "any such property" in section 630 were wide enough to include past officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 6 of the 1947 Act which provides for prosecution of an officer or employee of a Company for wrongfully withholding possession of such property. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words 'any such properties ' in sub section 2 of section 631 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employee but also to include future officers and servants of the Company; (ii) the legislature never intended to include all past officers, employees or employees of the respondent company within its ambit of Section 630(1)(b); (iii) the word 'any ' in section 6 should be interpreted as including past officers or employees. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words 'other employees ' in subsection (l) of Section 631 must take their colour from the context in which it appears. The whole object of enacting sub section(1), namely, to provide a summary procedure for retrieving the property and to prevent abuse of the property by an officer who is permitted to use any property of a public company during his employment, wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his service. [176F G] 2. The expression 'any past or present officer ' in Section 630 of H; 176A] 3. The word 'employee ' in the section means an officer of a corporation who has obtained possession of any property or of a concern in his possession knowingly applies it to purposes other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act.

The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was formed by the Maharaj who had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the said Sansthan. In the year of account 18,164 61 were purchased from the temple by one Vithal Rukhamai. The appellant 's father died in 1952. The widow of the Sansthan filed a suit for declaration that the Sansthan was not a public trust. The trial court held that the deity was a private property and not a private trust. On appeal the District Judge reversed the decision holding that the appellant was a public Trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and restored the order of the Charity Commissioner. The High Court in revision set aside the order passed by the District judge and held that it was a Public Trust under section 29 of the , and therefore the appellant 'was not a trustee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande. [523 B] (2) The expression "public trust" is a very important piece of evidence to show that a public temple is a private one. The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. [525 C D] (3) The definition of public trust contained in section 2 (13) and section 2 1(14) respectively of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, shows that the property has always been treated as trust property even by the Officer saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The definition is very wide in its application to a public charitable trust. [500 D E] (4) In view of the fact that the temple was dedicated for the Darshan by the appellant, the endowment was a religious endowment within the scope of section 29 and the High Court was right in holding that it had no appearance of any impediment or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the public extending over a long period. [511 C D; 512 A] (5) The position and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property had been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property was dealt with, or managed, by those who were entitled to worship at the shrine of the temple, the nature of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a public religious endowment. [506 B C] (6) The fact that a person has been appointed as manager of a temple does not make him a private or a body of persons interested. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public character without the least interference or restriction from the Temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the State of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the character of devolution being that of a religious trust. Therefore, in this case all the above tests are fulfilled. [605 C D]. (7) The properties in question were endowed for the worship of the public and the same had been managed by the saint. The fact of endowment was not such as to convert the gifts which was expressly in favor of the appellant.

The appellant was the sole proprietor of a business carried on under the name and style of Indestro Sales and Service Co. Ltd., Bombay, carrying on business in the City of Bombay. The respondent firm was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 58 by the Third Income Tax Officer, Cannanore, for the assessment year 1947 48. The appellant challenged the validity of the said assessment on the ground that section 46(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, under which the Income Tax officer issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay was void under article 13(1) of that Constitution in that the same was repugnant to article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that section 16 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, underwhich the warrant of arrest was issued by the Additional Collec tor of Bombay, was void and the same being repugnant to Article 14 of that Act, was not saved by article 21 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 13 of the Act was violative of article 21 inasmuch as it offended article 22(1), and (2) that section 17 of the City Land Reve nue Act, 1889, under Which the warrant for arrest was passed by the Collector was void in that it contravened article 14. HELD: The provisions of the State laws which prescribe that machinery are not incorporated in section 46 (2), do not violate article 21. They are not in terms and by themselves, they are concerned at all with the recovery of income tax demand. [157 E] The State laws prescribe the procedure for the recovery and have to be followed in accordance with the procedure prescribed by their own State laws as if those provisions were set out in the Indian Incometax Act in extenso and it is not possible to say that all the provisions of all the State law are, mutatis mutandis, to be read into section 46. [158 E] In the present case, the appellant had been arrested and detained for a longer period than six months and was being detained for more than the period limited by the Code of Civil Procedure for the detention of a judgment debtor in execution of a decree for an equal amount of money. The State law prescribes the procedure which is followed in the exercise of its powers under article 136 of the constitution.

The respondents were the owners of a Prince 's and Victoria Docks under which each shift consisted of 8 hours ' normal duty, 2 hours ' overtime and one hour 's overtime. The Trustees agreed to accept the hours of rest at fixed hours in the Alexandra Docks but at the Prince 'S guilty of the breach of the Act and the Rules. They were prosecuted for contravening section 3(1)(a) of the , and section 13(2) read with section 5 of the . The Tribunal held that the Union was not able to establish that the existing system of work required any modification, that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours off rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 51 of the are applicable to all factories irrespective of their location or their location. The Bombay Port Trust Employees ' Union vs The Employees of the Port of Bombay, ; , referred to. The Tribunal was right in holding that the union was not entitled to fix the number and hours of working in a six day week. The workers were entitled to three hours ' wages in accordance with section 51, but they did not do so. The period of leave at the beginning of a month is not a part of the normal working day. The hours of duty are only 8 hours for any day and work up to 9 hours on any day can be taken without paying overtime if the total number of days in the week does not exceed 48. The fact that the workers were required to work beyond 9 hours in a 12 hour shift, but he must pay a double rate for any hour or part of an hour of actual work in excess of 9 hours would not make him liable to pay overtime if his total number exceeded 48.

The appellant was the tenant of a accommodation in the first floor of the building. The respondent landlord filed an application for eviction under section 13(1)(i) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on the ground that the shop and the basement were separately let out to the appellant. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 will not apply to the premises in view of the language of sections 39 and 40 of the Act. The first appellate court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the second appeal on the view that since the premises were let out in June 1976, the provisions would not apply for 10 years from October 1, 1976 and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rights of parties will be governed on the basis of the date on which the suit was filed; (ii) even if the matter is pending in this Court and 10 years have elapsed since the date of the commencement of the proceedings, the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection under this section because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore it would not be possible for the appellant to get the benefit of the provisions contained in section 20(2) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The rights of the parties will depend on the date when the suit is filed or from such date of commencement of this Act i.e. 15th July 1972 and therefore, it cannot be said that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on the dates on which this Act came into force.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, who were the tenants under him and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The trial court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in view of section 3 of the Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as amended by the West Bengal Thika Tenants (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, which came into force on January 1, 1951. On appeal the High Court confirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of section 4 of the Act as amended in 1953; (2) the amendment of the West Thika tenancy Act by the Amending Act of 1953, had to be examined to show how far they disturb the rights of landlord to recover possession of the property from a person, who would be a thika tenant on 28th February 1949; and (3) the High court was in error in holding that the respondent could not be said to have acquired any of the grounds mentioned in section 3. HELD: (i) The amendment of 1956 had to proceed on the basis that he was such a tenant in 1949 with the result that he could claim the benefit under section 4. [184 B] (ii) Section 5(1) of the Calcutta Thika Tenant Act, 1948, as it stood at the relevant time, provided that "the provisions of this Act shall apply to all suits and proceedings including proceedings for eviction of a thikika tenant which are pending on the date of commencement of this Ordinance. " The respondent was therefore entitled to succeed in his suit. [185 G] (iii) Section 4 of Act of 1949 was prospective only, it could not apply to pre Act suits. The landlord had to establish that he had been so a thata tenant in view Of section 3 and the only qualification was that even if the suit had been filed before the Act but was not disposed of by that date, the landlord had also to establish the existence of one of the ground specified in section 4(1). [185 B C] (iv) The High Court was right in holding on the view that sections 4 and 5 being prospective only it could apply to the case.

The State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference to the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against Rs.120 300 to Section Officers. The Committee recommended for approval of the pay scales of the Bench Secretaries and also recommended that the nomenclature of posts of Bench Secretaries be changed from Rs. 120 300 to Rs.200 400. The High Court suggested a uniform pay scale for all the posts of Benches of the High Court. The State Government accepted this recommendation and issued an order dated July 2, 1976 directing that all Bench Secretaries irrespective of their grades should be given the same pay scale which is being given to Superintendents i.e. Rs. 150 350. The appellant State Government filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the order of the Chief Justice. The learned Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court allowed the writ petition and directed that all Benches Secretaries irrespective on the basis of seniority alone, but on the ground that they were not entitled to the same scale of pay which was being given by Superintendents i,e. it was not open to them to have been given the similar scale of Pay as was being paid to Superintendents. The Division Bench also held that the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to be construed in the light of Article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the High Courts were not right in giving higher pay scale only to ten Judges and that the creation of two grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretary who are doing the same or similar work is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay for unequal work has to he construed in this first place. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal pay is a concomitant of Article14 of the constitution. But it follows naturally that equal pays for unequal works will be a negation of that right. [297G H] 2. The Court has completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules The merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification made under the rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the State Government has granted uniform pay scales for Bench Secretaries with effect from January 1, 1986. When Bench Secretaries Grade I acquire experience and also display more merit, they are appointed as Bench Secretaries grade I. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay Scale. [298H; 299A B] 3.

The appellant companies were incorporated under the . The State Government of Madhya Pradesh, in exercise of its powers under section 127A of the M.P. Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, framed a scheme for the development and administration of certain areas in the State. The scheme was published in the Gazette on June 24, 1976. The appellant companies challenged the validity of the scheme by filing writ petitions before the High Court of Madhya Bharat challenging the validity. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the scheme was not covered by the agreement of 1976 and therefore it was beyond the scope of section 127 A of the Act. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant companies it was contended that (i) since the appellant company was owned wholly by the Government of India, the lands were owned wholly and exclusively by the State Government; (ii) the provisions conferring powers of taxation under the aforesaid two Acts must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation and the Municipal Corporation was not competent to impose the property tax; (iii) since it was not liable to pay entry tax by reason of the agreement, on January 4, 1977 respondent 1 could not impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the Municipal Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that in the instant case, subsequent amendments made to the Municipal Corpora tion Act and the Municipalities Act will also apply to the power of taxation provided for in section 127(d). [14 B] (i)(a) The object of the two Acts is to provide for the improvement and administration by providing for the proper and scientific utilisation of coal resources. The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State Legislature loses its competence to pass the Act of 1973 it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof under which Special Area Development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. [14 C D] (b) The High Courts were right in taking the view that subsequent amendments brought about by the two enactments could not be availed of by respondent 1. [15 E F] (c) The State Legislature lost its competence in entering into the agreement with the appellant Companies, under which respondent 1 bound itself not to impose any tax whatsoever. [16 G] (d) The power conferred by the Act on the Central Government to impose property tax on lands and building is not in conflict with the power conferred upon the Union Government to regulate and develop the Coal Mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilization of coal resource. The paramount purpose behind the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957 is not to control the mining industry but to impose a duty on the owner of the land or building as the case may be for the purposes of that section a tenant of land or buildings or both who holds the same under a lease for an agreed period with a convenant for its renewal thereafter. [17 E F; 18 A] (2) The first contention is without substance and must fail. The second contention is that assuming that section 127B of the , was not applicable to the case, it was open to the State to impose tax on land and buildings in accordance with the provisions thereof, under sections 129 & 133 of that Acts. [18 C] (3) The Act is primarily concerned with the development, and regulation of declared industries and not with the ownership of industrial undertakings.

The appellant was granted a lease of certain slate quarries in his estate for five years in respect of the slate quarry. The lessee applied to the Government under section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, for a renewal of the lease and on December 27, 1955, the Board of Revenue passed an order declaring that the lease should be terminated without any compensation. On December 27 the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Board. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights which were created on or after July 1, 1945, could only be done under the third proviso to section 20 (1) and not under section 21(2). On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The words "such rights" in the third Proviso to section 7(1), refer to rights created after July I, 1945 mentioned in the previous proviso. The words 'such rights ' in the second proviso have reference to rights conferred on or before the date of the first proviso and not to those which are expressly mentioned in that proviso. (ii)The third proviso is merely declaratory and does not relate to the rights mentioned in section 20 of the Act. The effect of the second Proviso is that the Government must do something to avoid them. If the third, proviso also applies to such leases as the petitioners contended, then the Government could have exercised the right conferred on it by the second, proviso and therefore, the Government was bound to give three months ' notice. (iii)The words " such rights" refer to the right created after the first July 1. 1945, mentioned in sub section (2) must be read as a proviso not to the section but to the second. The third proviso does not apply to the present case because the third and the third provisos deal with the rights created before the notified date but after July lI, 1945 for a period exceeding one year.
